CHAPTER IV 


EFFECT OF DISCIPLINARY OR JUDICIAL PROCEEDINGS ON BENEFITS UNDER 
THE UNIFIED PENSION SCHEME 


20. Effect of compulsory retirement.- (1) A railway servant compulsorily retired from service 
as a penalty, may be granted, by the authority competent to impose such penalty, benefits at a rate 
not less than two thirds and not more than full admissible payout to him out of the individual 
corpus under the Unified Pension Scheme. 


Explanation. — For the purposes of this sub-rule “admissible payout” means the amount 
payable to a Unified Pension Scheme subscriber for life, in such proportion and in such manner 
as specified under the regulations. 


(2) The benefits under sub-rule (1) shall be paid to the railway servant in accordance with the 
regulations. 


(3) Whenever in the case of a railway servant, the President passes an order (whether under 
original, appellate or in exercise of power of review) awarding benefits less than full benefits, the 
Union Public Service Commission shall be consulted before such order is passed. 


(4) The order passed under this rule shall be without prejudice to any order passed under the 
Railway Services (Payment of Gratuity under National Pension System) Rules, 2025 for grant of 
gratuity to the railway servant compulsorily retired from railway service. 


(5) The assured payout granted on compulsory retirement from service shall not be less than 
the minimum payout admissible under the Unified Pension Scheme. 


21. Effect of dismissal or removal. -(1) A railway servant, who is dismissed or 
removed from service shall forfeit assured payouts arising out of the individual corpus under the 
Unified Pension Scheme: 


Provided that on forfeiture of the assured payout under the Unified Pension Scheme on 
dismissal or removal from service, the accumulated pension wealth in the individual corpus under 
the Unified Pension Scheme of the subscriber, shall be payable in lump sum to the subscriber or 
in the event of death of subscriber, to the legally married spouse, or in the absence thereof to the 
legal heir(s) under the regulations. 


(2) The order passed under this rule shall. be without prejudice to any order passed under the 
Railway Services (Payment of Gratuity under National Pension System) Rules, 2025 for grant of 
gratuity to the railway servant dismissed or removed from government service. 


22. Effect of departmental or judicial proceedings pending on retirement.- (1) Where 
departmental or judicial proceedings, which were instituted while the subscriber was in service 
but are not concluded before retirement, such railway servant on retirement from service on 
attaining the age of superannuation, shall be entitled to the accumulated pension wealth in the 
individual corpus under the Unified Pension Scheme, to be paid in lump sum in accordance with 
the regulations and shall not be paid any assured payout arising out of the individual corpus under 
the Unified Pension Scheme: 


Provided that departmental proceedings instituted under rule 11 of the Railway Servants 
(Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1968, while the railway servant was in service and continued after 
retirement, or the judicial proceedings instituted after retirement of the subscriber, shall not affect 
the assured payout arising out of the individual corpus under the Unified Pension Scheme payable 
to the subscriber in accordance with the regulations. 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 45 


(2) The departmental proceedings referred to in sub-rule (1), shall, after the retirement of the 
railway servant, be deemed to be proceedings under rule 5 of the Railway Services (Payment of 
Gratuity under National Pension System) Rules, 2025 and shall be continued and concluded by 
the authority by which they were initiated in the same manner as if the railway servant had 
continued in service. 


(3) (a) On conclusion of departmental or judicial proceedings, where the railway servant is 
fully exonerated from all charges, the railway servant shall have an option for availing assured 
payout under the Unified Pension Scheme based on the notional value of his individual corpus 
and benchmark corpus at the time of retirement in accordance with the regulations and on exercise 
of option for assured payout, the railway servant shall deposit the value of benchmark corpus or 
part thereof, not less than forty per cent. of the benchmark corpus, calculated notionally at the 
time of his retirement, along with applicable rate of interest and manner as in the case of Public 
Provident Fund deposits from time to time and the admissible assured payout shall be payable 
from the date of his retirement. 


(b) Arrears of assured payout shall be paid to the subscriber along with interest at the rate of 
interest and manner as in the case of Public Provident Fund deposits from time to time. 


(c) On the death of Railway servant during the pendency of the departmental or judicial 
proceedings after his retirement, the legally married spouse of the Railway servant at the time of 
retirement shall have an option for availing assured payout under the Unified Pension Scheme 
based on the notional value of individual corpus and benchmark corpus of the subscriber at the 
time of retirement in accordance with the regulations. 


(d) on exercise of option for assured payout, spouse shall deposit the value of benchmark 
corpus or part thereof, not less than forty per cent. of the benchmark corpus, calculated notionally 
at the time of his retirement, along with applicable rate of interest and manner as in the case of 
Public Provident Fund deposits from time to time and the admissible assured payout shall be 
payable from the date of retirement of subscriber and arrears of admissible assured payout payable 
to the subscriber and the spouse as per the regulations, shall be paid to the legally wedded spouse 
along with interest at the rate of interest and manner as in the case of Public Provident Fund 
deposits from time to time. 


(e) In case, a Railway servant dies after retirement without receiving the accumulated pension 
wealth in individual corpus admissible under Unified Pension Scheme or the arrears of assured 
payout due to him, or the legally married spouse of the subscriber dies before receiving the arrears 
of assured payout or family payout under Unified Pension Scheme, the accumulated pension 
wealth or the arrears of assured payout shall be disbursed to the legal heir(s) of the subscriber. 


(4) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-rule (1) any action taken in such cases in respect 
of gratuity and other retirement benefits not covered by these rules and those benefits shall be 
regulated in accordance with the rules as applicable to such benefits. 


23. Debarring spouse from receiving assured payout. - (1)If the spouse of the subscriber, 
who in the event of death of the subscriber is eligible to receive family payout under the 
regulations, is charged with the offence of murdering the subscriber or for abetting in the 
commission of such an offence, his or her claim to receive family payout shall remain suspended 
till the conclusion of the criminal proceedings instituted against him or her. 


(2) If on the conclusion of the criminal proceedings referred to in sub-rule (1), the person 
concerned, — 


(a) is convicted for the murder or abetting in the murder of the subscriber, he or she 
shall be debarred from receiving family payout under the Unified Pension Scheme; or 


(b) — is acquitted of the charge of murdering or abetting in the murder of the government 
subscriber, the assured payout shall be paid from the date it was due to him or her along 
with the interest at Public Provident Fund rates on the arrear of payout, in accordance with 
the regulations:

Provided that on debarring from the family payout arising out of the individual corpus 
under the Unified Pension Scheme on conclusion of the criminal proceedings referred to in sub- 
tule (1), the accumulated wealth in the individual corpus under Unified Pension Scheme of the 
subscriber, shall be payable in lump sum to the legal heir (s)of the subscriber. 


CHAPTER V 
PROCEDURE 


24. Preparation of list of subscriber due for retirement. - (1)Every Head of Department 
shall have a list prepared in every three months, that is, on the Ist January, 1“ April, 17 July and 
17 October each year of all subscribers who are due to retire within the next twelve to fifteen 
months from that date. 


(2) A copy of every such list, as specified in sub-rule (1), shall be supplied to the Pay and 
Accounts Officer concerned not later than the 31% January, 307 April, 31% July or the 317 October, 
as the case may be, of that year. 


(3) Inthe case ofa subscriber retiring for reasons other than by way of superannuation, the Head 
of Office shall promptly inform the Drawing and Disbursing Officer and the Pay and Accounts 
Officer concerned, as soon as the fact of such retirement came to his notice. 


(4) Acopy of intimation sent by the Head of Office to the Pay and Accounts Officer under sub- 
tule (3) shall also be endorsed to the Directorate of Estates or to the office concerned or to the 
office concerened for allotment of Railway accommodation, if the subscriber concerned is an 
allottee of Government accommodation or Railway accommodation. 


25. Intimation to the Directorate of Estates or to the office concerned or to the concerned 
office of Railway regarding issue of "no demand certificate".- (1)The Head of Office shall 
write to the Directorate of Estates or to the office concerned or in the case of railway 
accommodation to the concerned office at least one year before the anticipated date of retirement 
of the subscriber who was or is in occupation of a Government accommodation or Railway 
accommodation, as the case may be (hereinafter referred to as allottee) for issuing a No Demand 
Certificate! in respect of the period preceding eight months of the retirement of the allottee. 


(2) On receipt of the intimation under sub-rule (1), the Directorate of Estates or the office 
concerned or the office concerned of railway accommodation shall take further action as required. 


26. Submission of claim for benefits under the Unified Pension Scheme on superannuation. 
- (1) A subscriber shall have the option for submission of claim for benefit under the Unified 
Pension Scheme through a mode, as specified by the Authority from time to time. 


(2) Every subscriber shall, on retirement from service, submit duly filled withdrawal form 
prescribed by the Authority along with the documents mentioned in the withdrawal form in 
accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development 
Authority (Operationalisation of Unified Pension Scheme under National Pension System) 
Regulations, 2025. 


27. Subscribers on deputation. - (1)In the case of subscriber who retires while on deputation 
to another Central Government Department, action to authorise benefits in accordance with the 
provisions of this rule shall be taken by the Head of Office of the parent Department . 


(2) In the case of a subscriber who retires from service, while on deputation to a State Government 
or while on foreign service, action to authorise benefits in accordance with the provisions of this 
rule shall be taken by the Head of Office or the Cadre controlling authority which sanctioned 
deputation to the State Government or to foreign service. 


(3) In the case of Central Government employees belonging to various Ministries or Departments 
who happen to be on deputation to Railways at the time of their retirement, action to authorise 
benefits in accordance with the provisions of this rule shall be taken by the head of office of the 
parent Department.

28. Oversight mechanism.- (1) The accounts directorate of the Ministry of Railways (Railway 
Board) shall constitute the Unified Pension Scheme Oversight mechanism in accordance with the 
instructions issued by the Government from time to time, to, - 


(a) ensure the contribution of employees and the government are credited without delay to the 
individual corpus under Unified Pension Scheme financial architecture both in case of existing 
employees and employees newly recruited from time to time and the existing system and 
procedure being followed for the purpose shall be monitored effectively to ensure that no delay in 
credit of the contributions takes place; 


(b) ensure that in case any grievance by any employee is received in regard to delay in credit of 
contribution, either directly from the employee or through the Authority, the same has been looked 
into and disposed of in a manner to the satisfaction of the concerned employee; 


(c) other matters as having a bearing on the issue of crediting or remittance of Unified Pension 
Scheme contributions. 


(2) The accounts directorate of the Ministry of Railways (Railway Board), shall submit a 
status report in every six month to the Department of Pension & Pensioners’ Welfare (DoP&PW) 
with respect to the result of the monitoring carried out through the above oversight mechanism 
with concluding remarks whether the Unified Pension Scheme contributions are being credited on 
time and in case of any slippages, the details of the action taken. 


CHAPTER VI 
MISCELLANEOUS 


29. Date of retirement to be notified. - When a subscriber retires from service,— 
(a) A notification in the Official Gazette in the case of a Gazetted subscriber; and 
(b) An office order in the case of a Non-Gazetted subscriber, 


shall be issued specifying the date of retirement within a week of such date and a copy of every 
such notification or office order, as the case may be, shall be forwarded immediately to the Pay 
and Accounts Officer. 


30. Interpretation. -Where any doubt arises as to the interpretation of these rules, it shall 
be referred to the Ministry of Railways (Railway Board), for decision and the Ministry of 
Railways (Railway Board) shall take decision after consulting the Department of Pension and 
Pensioners’ Welfare of the Government of India. 


31. Power to relax. — Where the competent authority is satisfied that the operation of any 
of these rules causes undue hardship in any particular case, that authority, may for reasons, to 
be recorded in writing, refer the Ministry of Railways (Railway Board) for dispensing with or 
relaxing the requirements of that rule to such extent and subject to such exceptions and 
conditions as it may consider necessary for dealing with the case in a just and equitable manner. 


(2) The Ministry of Railways (Railway Board) shall examine each such case and arrange to 
communicate the sanction of the President to the proposed dispensation or relaxation, as it may 
consider necessary keeping in view of the merits of each case and keeping in view of another 
statutory provisions: 


Provided that no such order shall be made without concurrence of the Department of 
Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare, in the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, 
Government of India and the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance.

32. Power of Central Government to provide for residual matters. - (1) Any related 
issues not specifically covered in these rules, shall be decided in terms of the relevant provisions 
in this regard contained in the Railway Services (Implementation of National Pension System ) 
Rules, 2025, the Railway Services (Payment of Gratuity under National Pension System ) Rules, 
2025, the Railway Services (Pension) Rules, 2026, Code or any general or special order issued 
by the Government, provided it is not repugnant to or inconsistent with the provisions of these 
rules. 


(2) The Central Government may issue orders or instructions to regulate any matter for 
which there is no provision in the rules made or deemed to have been made under these rules 
and, until such rules are made, such matters shall be regulated as per orders or instructions issued 
from time to time. 


33. Repeal and saving. - On the commencement of these rules, every order, instruction or 
Office Memorandum in force immediately before such commencement shall, in so far as it 
provides for any of the matters contained in these rules, cease to operate and anything done or 
any action taken under those order, instruction or Office Memorandum shall be deemed to have 
been taken under the corresponding provisions of these rules.

MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS

NOTIFICATION 
New Delhi, the 17th September, 2026 
Notice under Section 20E of the Railway Act, 1989 


S.O. 5187(E).— Whereas, by the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Railways (East 
Central Railway), number 8.0. 4223(E), dated the 24th September, 2025 published in the Gazette of India, 
Extraordinary, Part-II, section 3, Sub-section (2), dated the 24th September and issued under sub-section (1) of 20 (A) 
of the Railway Act, 1989 (24 of 1989) (hereinafter referred as the said Act), the Central Government declared its 
intention to acquire the land in the schedule annexed to the said notification for the purpose of the Special Railway 
Project namely “Construction of New Line between Aurangabad Terminal to Anugrah Narayan Road (12.906 km.)” 
of East Central Railway, in the District Aurangabad in the State of Bihar. 


And whereas, the substance of the said notification was published in daily local newspapers, namely, Prabhat 
Khabar & The Times of India (Patna Edition) dated 15th November 2025, under sub-section (4) of section 20A of the 
said Act; 


And whereas, objections were received, Competent Authority has heard the objections and orders have been 
passed in terms of section 20 D of the said act; 


And whereas, in pursuance of sub-section (1) of section 20E of the said Act, the Competent Authority has 
submitted its report to the Central Government. 


Now therefore, upon receipt of the report of the Competent Authority and in exercise of the powers conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 20E of the said Act, the Central Government hereby declares that the lands specified in 
the Schedule annexed hereto shall be acquired for the aforesaid purpose. 


And further, in the pursuance of sub-section (2) of section 20E of the said Act, the Central Government 
hereby declares that on publication of this notification in the Official Gazette the land specified in the Schedule 
annexed hereto shall vest absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances.

MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(South Central Railway) 
NOTIFICATION 
Secunderabad, the 21st September, 2026 


5.0. 5195(E).— In exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (I) of section 20A of the Railways 
Act, 1989 (24 of 1989) (hereafter referred as in as the said Act), Central Government after being satisfied 
that for the public purpose, the land, the brief description of which is given in the schedule annexed hereto, 
is required for execution of the Special Railway Project, Mudkhed - Dhone Doubling in of Track between 
Sirnapalli and Uppalavai Stations in Kamareddy district in the state of Telangana, hereby declares its 
intention to acquire such land: 


Any person interested in the said land may, within a period of thirty days from the date of publication 
of this notification in the official gazette, raise objection to the acquisition and use of such land for the 
aforesaid purpose under sub- section (1) of section 20D of the said act: 


Every such objection shall be made to the competent authority, namely Revenue Divisional Officer 
and Land Acquisition Officer, Kamareddy in writing and shall set out the grounds thereof and the competent 
authority shall give the objector an opportunity of being heard, either in person or by legal practitioner and 
may, after hearing all such objections and after making such further enquiry, if any as the competent authority 
thinks necessary, by order, either allow or disallow the objections. 


Any order made by the competent authority under sub section (II) of section 20(D) of the said act 
shall be final. 


The land plans and other details of the land under this notification are available and can be inspected 
by the interested person at the aforesaid office of the competent authority.

ORDER 


The election of first respondent from Alappuzha Parliamentary Constituency on 26.04.2024 is under challenge 
in this election petition filed by the defeated candidate who secured the highest number of votes among the remaining 
10 candidates. 


2. The ground alleged for setting aside the election of the first respondent, and for declaration of the petitioner 
as duly elected, is corrupt practice as envisaged under Sections 123(3), 123(3-A) and 123(4) of the Representation of 
People Act, 1951 (for short "RP Act’). 


3. The Registry noted as many as 12 defects in the filing of this election petition and placed the matter before 
Bench, by assigning a filing number, for deciding whether the election petition could be received to files. In the 
meanwhile, the learned counsel for the petitioner sought multiple adjournments for advancing arguments against the 
aforesaid objections raised by the Registry, due to the reason that he was indisposed pursuant to a bypass surgery. Thus, 
the status of the case remained as unnumbered Election Petition. While so, the first respondent appeared through counsel 
and filed I.A.No.1/2025 for dismissal of the Election Petition in limine. 


4. Heard the learned counsel for the petitioner, and the learned counsel for the first respondent. 


5. At the time of arguments, the learned counsel for the first respondent submitted that the maintainability of 
this Election Petition is at stake, not only due to the defects noted by the Registry but also for the absence of any cause 
of action to entertain such a petition. Adverting to the 12 defects noted in tabular form by the Registry, the learned 
counsel for the first respondent pointed out that the defect noted as Serial No.4 thereunder, is incurable. 


6. The aforesaid defect noted under SI.No.4 pertained to the failure of the election petitioner to mention about 
the Annexures produced by him as 'H' to 'M' in the affidavit filed under Form No.25. The Registry has pointed out that, 
as per Rule 94A of the Conduct of Election Rules, details regarding each and every paragraph of the petition including 
documents, shall be mentioned in the affidavit. 


7. Among the 20 documents produced by the petitioner as Annexures A to M, Annexures A to G related to the 
screenshots of the videos alleged to have been uploaded and published by the election agents and associates of the first 
respondent in social media, and its English translations. Annexure H is a compact disc which is said to be containing 
the videos described as Annexures A to G. Annexure I is a certificate as required under Section 63 of the Bharatiya 
Sakshya Adhiniyam in respect of Annexure H. Annexure-J is the true copy of a hash report in respect of the seven 
videos said to have been preserved in Annexure-H. Annexure-K is also a certificate pertaining to the seven videos said 
to have been preserved in Annexure-H compact disc. Annexure-L is the hash report prepared by another person, in 
respect of the seven videos said to have been preserved in Annexure-H compact disc. Annexure-M is the true copy of 
the challan dated 17.07.2024. 


8. The requirement to file an affidavit in the prescribed form in support of corrupt practice alleged in an election 
petition, is contained in the proviso to Section 83(1) RP Act. Rule 94A of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961, requires 
that the aforesaid affidavit shall be in Form No.25. A perusal of Form No.25 would make it clear that the affidavit so 


4 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART II—SEC. 3(ii1)] 


filed should contain solemn affirmation that the statements made in the relevant paragraphs of the election petition about 
the commission of corrupt practice, and the particulars of the corrupt practice mentioned in the relevant paragraphs of 
the election petition and that of the schedule annexed thereto, are true to the knowledge and information of the deponent. 
As far as the present case is concerned, the Annexures produced by the election petitioner as A to G are screen-shot 
documents pertaining to the corrupt practice alleged to have been committed by the agents and associates of the returned 
candidate. Annexure-H is the compact disc which is said to contain the videos of the corrupt practice described in 
Annexures-A to G. The certificates, and hash reports mentioned as Annexures-I to L also relate to the documents which 
the petitioner has produced as Annexures-A to H. That being so, the failure of the petitioner to mention about Annexures- 
H to L in the affidavit filed would clearly amount to a violation of the requirement of Rule 94A of the Conduct of 
Election Rules, 1961. However, the non-mentioning of Annexure-M which is true copy of the challan showing the 
remittance of the prescribed fees by the petitioner, need not be mentioned in the affidavit, since it does not relate to the 
corrupt practice alleged in this election petition. 


9. Now, the question to be looked into is whether the infraction of law in the above regard is sufficient to 
dismiss the election petition in limine. As per Section 86(1) of the RP Act, the High Court shall dismiss an election 
petition which does not comply with the provisions Section 81 or Section 82 or Section 117. Since the violation alleged 
is one relating to the non-compliance of the proviso to Section 83(1) of the RP Act, there is no applicability of the 
mandate contained in Section 86(1) of the said Act, which requires the High Court to dismiss the election petition. Thus, 
the position that emerges is that the failure of the petitioner to mention in the affidavit about Annexures-H to L can only 
be taken as a curable defect, and there is absolutely no scope of dismissal of the election petition at the threshold for the 
omission in the above regard, 


10. As rightly pointed out by the learned counsel for the election petitioner, the proposition of law in this regard 
is laid down in the Constitution Bench decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in 7.M. Jacob v. C. Paulose & Ors. [(1999) 
4 SCC 274], and various subsequent decisions thereafter up to Thangjam Arun Kumar v. Yumkham Erabot Singh & 
Ors. [AIR 2023 SCC 4531]. Therefore, the challenge against the maintainability of the election petition in view of the 
aforesaid defect noted by the Registry, is totally untenable, since it is only a curable defect. The other 11 defects noted 
by the Registry are also trivial in nature, and hence those defects cannot be termed as substantial defects fatal to the very 
maintainability of the election petition. 


11. The learned counsel for the first respondent pointed out that the corrupt practices alleged under Section 123 
of the RP Act can only be those acts committed after the submission of nomination by the returned candidate against 
whom the election petition is filed. Adverting to the definition of "candidate" as envisaged under section 79(b) of the 
RP Acct, the learned counsel for the first respondent argued that before the submission of nomination, the first respondent 
cannot be termed as a candidate, and hence the acts alleged to have been committed prior to the submission of 
nomination of the first respondent will not come within the purview of the objectionable acts contained under Sections 
123(3), 123(3-A) & 123(4) of the RP Act. The law laid down by the Constitution Bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain [AIR 1975 SCC 2299] which has been followed by the Apex Court in Subhash 
Desai v. Sharad J. Rao [1994 Suppl. (2) SCC 446], Mohan Rawale v. Damodar Tatyaba [(1994) 2 SCC 392], 
Chandrakantha Goyal v. Sohan Singh Jodh Singh Kohli (1996) 1 SCC 378] and Manohar Joshi v. Nitin Bhaurao 
Patil [((1996) 1 SCC 169] are relied on by the learned counsel for the first respondent in support of the argument that 
the allegations pertaining to the objectionable acts committed by the agents and associates of the first respondent, prior 
to the date of submission of nomination by the first respondent, cannot be termed as corrupt practices envisaged under 
Sections 123(3), 123(3-A) & 123(4) of the RP Act. 


12. There is absolutely no need for this Court to elaborate upon the aforesaid decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court since the law is now trite that the corrupt practices envisaged under Section 123 of the RP Act for challenging the 
election of a returned candidate can only be those acts committed by the candidate, his election agents or associates after 
the date of submission of nomination by that candidate. As far as the present case is concerned, all the allegations 
levelled by the petitioner in this election petition pertain to those acts allegedly committed by the agents and associates 
of the first respondent even before the publication of the election notification on 28.03.2024. Therefore, it cannot be 
said that the allegations levelled by the petitioner in his election petition to set aside the election of the first respondent 
and to declare him as the duly elected candidate, would come within the purview of the corrupt practices envisaged 
under Section 123 of the RP Act. 


13. Now, the next question to be looked into is whether the aforesaid reason is a ground to dismiss the election 
petition at the threshold. The learned counsel for the first respondent, by adverting to Section 87 of the RP Act, pointed 
out that an election petition has to be tried by this Court in accordance with the procedure applicable under the Code of 
Civil Procedure, 1908, to the extent possible, and hence if the election petition does not disclose a cause of action, it has 
to be rejected at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11(a) of the said Code. It is further pointed out by the learned 
counsel for the first respondent that, when the averments in the election petition do not constitute any legally sustainable 
grounds to set aside the election of the returned candidate, it could only be said that the said petition does not disclose 
a cause of action. Thus, according to the learned counsel for the first respondent, the election petition has to be rejected. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(iii)] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 5 


14. Per contra, it is argued by the learned counsel for the petitioner that the election petition is not liable to be 
rejected at the very inception, since the petitioner is entitled to incorporate appropriate allegations in the said petition 
by way of amendment in the further course of procedures. I am not impressed by the aforesaid argument of the learned 
counsel for the petitioner, since the law prohibits the petitioner from making such amendments in the election petition 
in respect of material aspects which he has omitted to incorporate at the time of filing of that petition. 


15. The learned counsel for the first respondent brought to my notice the decisions rendered by the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court in Anil Vasudev Salgaonkar v. Naresh Kushali Shigaonkar [(2009) 9 SCC 310] and G.M. Siddeshwar 
v. Prasanna Kumar [(2013)4 SCC 776] wherein it has been held in unequivocal terms that an election petition can be 
summarily dismissed in exercise of the relevant provisions of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, if it does not furnish any 
cause of action. In paragraph No.52 of G.M. Siddeshwar (supra), it has been observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
as follows: 


"52. The principles emerging from these decisions are that although non-compliance with the 
provisions of Section 83 of the Act is a curable defect, yet there must be substantial compliance with 
the provisions thereof. However, if there is total and complete non-compliance with the provisions of 
Section 83 of the Act, then the petition cannot be described as an election petition and may be 
dismissed at the threshold." 


16. Going by the settled principles of law laid down by the Hon'ble supreme court in G. 14. Siddeshwar & Anil 
Vasudev Salgaonkar (supra), the present election petition cannot be entertained, since the averments contained in it, 
even if accepted as such, will not constitute any of the grounds envisaged under Section 123 of the RP Act to set aside 
the election of the first respondent. Since the election petition is yet to be numbered, there is no scope for a dismissal. 
The proper course to be adopted is a rejection of the election petition. 


In the result, the election petition stands rejected under Order VII Rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 
1908.

MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
[North Western Railway (Construction Organization)] 
NOTIFICATION 

Jaipur, the 24th September, 2026 
७.0. 5293 (E).— Whereas, by the notification of the Government of India, in the Ministry of Railways 
(North Western Railway, Construction organisation), Notification number, 5.0. 77I(E)dated the 07th April, 2026 
published in Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, section 3 Sub-section (ii), dated the 8th April, 2026(hereinafter 
referred to as the said notification) under sub-section (i) of section 20A of the Railways (Amendment) Act, 989 
(24of 989) (hereinafter referred to as the said Act), the Central Government declares its intention to acquire the land 
specified in the schedule annexed to the said notification for the purpose of execution, maintenance, management and 
operation of Special Railway Project, namely “Doubling between Ajmer-Chanderiya section (78.28km)” of 


Ajmer Division of North Western Railway” in the state of Rajasthan. 


And whereas, the substance of the said notification was published in daily newspapers namely 


“DainikBhaskar” and “Dainik Navjyoti” Dated 3"April-2026under sub section (4) of section 20A of the said Act; 


And whereas, the objections received were diposed off with suitable reply within the stipulated time periodby 


Competent Authority andaccordingly orders have been passed. 


And, whereas, in pursuance of sub-section (l) of section 20E of the said Act, the competent authority 


hassubmitted its report to the Central Government; 


Now, therefore, upon receipt of the said report of the competent authority, and in exercise of the 
powersconferred by sub-section () of section 20E of the said Act, the Central Government hereby declare that the 


landsspecified in the schedule annexed hereto shall be acquired for the aforesaid purpose; 


And, further, in pursuance of sub-section (2) of section 20E of the said Act, The Central Government 
herbydeclares that on publication of the notification in the official Gazette, the land specified in the schedule annexed 


heretoshall vest absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances.

S.O. 530I(E).— Whereas, by the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Railways

section 3 Sub-section (ii), dated the 09" October 2025 (hereinafter referred to as the said notification) and 
issued under sub-section () of section 20A of the Railway Act, 989 (24 of 989) (hereinafter referred to as 
the said Act), the Central Government declares its intention to acquire the land specified in the schedule 
annexed to the said notification for the purpose of execution, maintenance, management and operation of 
Special Railway Project, namely “Manmad-Indore New Line (New Line between Manmad to New Dhule 
and Nardana to Dr. Ambedkar Nagar (309.43 Kms)” in the District of Nashik & Dhule of Maharashtra 
State & Badwani, Khargone, Dhar & Indore District of Madhya Pradesh State. 


And whereas, the substance of the said notification was published in for Sub-Divisional Officer 
(Revenue), Kasrawad Madhya Pradesh in daily newspapers namely “Times of India” & “Dhruva Vani” 
Dated ]0-2-2025 under sub section (4) of section 20A of the said Act. 


And no objections were received. 


And whereas, in pursuance of sub-section 20E of the said Act, the competent authority has submitted 
its report to the Central Government. 


Now therefore, upon receipt of the report of the Competent Authority and in exercise of the powers 
conferred by sub-section () of section 20E of the said Act, the Central Government hereby declares that the 
lands specified in the schedule annexed here to shall be acquired for the aforesaid purpose. 


And further, in pursuance of sub-section (2) of section 20E of the said Act, the Central Government 
hereby declares that on publication of this notification in the official Gazette, the land specified in the 
schedule annexed hereto shall vest absolutely in the Central government free from all encumbrances.

Rule 2(b) of the Anti-Dumping Rules defines domestic industry as under: 


“(b) “domestic industry” means the domestic producers as a whole engaged in 
the manufacture of the like article and any activity connected therewith or those 
whose collective output of the said article constitutes a major proportion of the 
total domestic production of that article except when such producers are related 
to the exporters or importers of the alleged dumped article or are themselves 
importers thereof in such case the term ‘domestic industry’ may be construed as 
referring to the rest of the producers ”’.

The injury is evident not only for the applicants collectively but also for 
individual producers. Payal Plastichem commenced production of the subject 
goods in 2024-25, following which subject imports increased significantly. 
The dumped imports undercut and depressed its prices, compelling it to reduce 
prices and resort to imports instead of domestic production. Likewise, despite 
sufficient capacity and growing demand, the production and domestic sales of 
Payal Polyplast declined during the injury period, and it was forced to reduce 
its selling prices beyond the decline in raw material costs. 

IGPL submitted that despite investing approximately 2200 crore in 
establishing production facilities for the subject goods, the continued influx of 
dumped imports threatens the commercial viability of its investment by 
preventing recovery of costs. It has therefore supported the imposition of anti- 
dumping duty on the subject imports. 

Not all injury parameters are required to deteriorate simultaneously for a 
finding of material injury. Although the domestic industry-maintained 
production and sales volumes by reducing prices, such volume performance 
came at the cost of severe deterioration in profitability and other financial 
parameters, consistent with WTO jurisprudence and the decision in Reliance 
Industries Ltd. v. Designated Authority. 

The decline in capacity utilisation is not attributable to capacity expansion. 
The expansion was undertaken in anticipation of increasing demand. Even 
after excluding the expanded capacities, the domestic industry continued to 
operate below optimal utilisation. In the absence of dumped imports, the 
domestic industry would have achieved significantly higher capacity 
utilisation, as demonstrated by its historical performance. 

The injury is not attributable to contraction in demand. Demand for the subject 
goods remained healthy during the injury period and has increased further in 
the post-POI period. Even during the temporary decline in demand, subject 
imports increased while the domestic industry-maintained sales only by 
sacrificing prices and profitability. 

The Annual Reports and CRISIL reports relied upon by the interested parties 
relate to the overall operations of the companies covering multiple products 
and are therefore not representative of the performance of the subject goods. 
The applicants have furnished segregated injury and cost information 
exclusively relating to the subject goods, which may be verified by the 
Authority. 

The injury is not attributable to alternative factors such as plant shutdowns, 
commercialisation of the new plant, inter-company loans, exchange rate 
fluctuations, diversification into specialty products, cost restructuring, 
preference for non-phthalate plasticizers, cyclical raw material prices or 
imports from non-subject countries. In particular, no shutdown due to raw 
material shortage occurred during the POI; imports from Turkey were 
negligible and imports from Korea RP were at non-injurious prices; exchange 
rate fluctuations did not materially affect costs or borrowings; there was no

internal cost restructuring or inefficiency; and no evidence has been produced 
to establish cyclical movement in raw material prices. Demand for the subject 
goods has continued to increase despite changing customer preferences. 

xviii. The decline in productivity, wages and employment does not negate the 
existence of injury, as these parameters depend upon several business factors. 
Further, the interested parties have taken contradictory positions by 
simultaneously alleging declining productivity and increased economies of 
scale. These parameters must therefore be considered together with the 
deterioration in profitability, prices and other injury indicators. 

XIX. The inverted duty structure is not the cause of injury. The domestic industry 
remained profitable despite the same duty structure in earlier years and 
suffered injury only after the surge in dumped imports. The inverted duty 
structure is a structural business reality and does not constitute an inefficiency. 
The anti-dumping duty should therefore adequately redress the injury caused 
by dumped imports rather than penalise the domestic industry for structural 
disadvantages. 

x, The non-injurious price must be determined on the basis of the verified cost of 
production of the domestic industry in accordance with Annexure III to the 
Rules. There is no legal requirement to optimise costs by adopting the costs of 
other producers. Optimisation is warranted only where inefficiencies exist, and 
no such inefficiencies have been established in the present case. Similarly, 
there is no legal basis for excluding the costs of a new producer while 
determining the non-injurious price. The Supreme Court in Reliance Industries 
Ltd. v. Designated Authority has recognised that the determination of non- 
injurious price should not discriminate against new producers. Further, start-up 
costs have been capitalised in accordance with Indian Accounting Standard-6 
and therefore do not inflate the cost of production or the non-injurious price.

determinative of injury.

Currency fluctuation 

The other interested parties have submitted that the domestic industry has incurred 
material injury on account of currency fluctuations. The Authority notes that no 
evidence has been placed on record in support of the claim. The Authority has 
nevertheless examined the submission. The Indian Rupee depreciated from %75.37 per 
US$ in 202-22 to %85.43 per US$ in the period of investigation, being a depreciation 
of about 3%. Such depreciation increases the rupee cost of the imported inputs of the 
domestic industry, but increases the rupee landed price of the subject imports to the 
same extent, and its effect is therefore neutral as between the domestic industry and the 
importer. It is noted that the landed price of the subject imports declined by 24% in 
rupee terms as against 33% in US Dollar terms, the difference being wholly attributable 
to the depreciation, so that the exchange rate movement has cushioned rather than 
accentuated the decline in the landed price. Examining the submission independently of 
the exchange rate, it is noted that the raw material cost of the domestic industry, 
expressed in US Dollar terms, declined to a lesser extent over the injury period than the 
landed price of the subject imports, which declined by 33% over the same period. The 
landed price has therefore declined to a greater extent than the cost of inputs even after 
the exchange rate is eliminated from the comparison. The Authority accordingly 
concludes to hold that the injury suffered by the domestic industry is not attributable to 
currency fluctuation.

Examination by the Authority 


The Authority notes that the primary objective of anti-dumping duties is to rectify the 
injury inflicted upon the domestic industry by the unjust trade practices of dumping, 
thereby fostering an environment of open and equitable competition in the Indian 
market. The imposition of anti-dumping measures is not designed to curtail imports 
from the subject country arbitrarily. Rather, it is a mechanism to ensure a level playing 
field. 


The Authority acknowledges that imposition of anti-dumping duties can affect prices in 
India. However, it is crucial to note that the essence of fair competition in the Indian 
market will remain unscathed by the imposition of these measures. Far from 
diminishing competition, the imposition of anti-dumping measures serves to prevent the 
accrual of unfair advantages through dumping practices. Thus, anti-dumping duties are 
not a hindrance but a facilitator of fair-trade practices Anti-dumping measures protect 
fair trade and ensure that consumers continue to have access to a wide range of these 
products.

G. METHODOLOGY 


34. Section 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, 975 read with the Rules governs the 
determination of a countervailable subsidy. A subsidy is said to exist where there is a financial 
contribution by a government or public body, or income or price support, which confers a benefit 
upon the recipient, and the subsidy is specific within the meaning of Article 2 of the SCM 
Agreement. 


35. Article 4 of the SCM Agreement provides guidelines and methodology for calculating 
the benefit to the recipient and requires that any method used by the investigating authority be 
provided for in national legislation or implementing regulations and that its application in each 
particular case be transparent and adequately explained. In accordance with that requirement, the 
Rules lay down the methodology for determining the quantum of subsidisation, and the 
determination in this investigation is in accordance with those guidelines. 


84 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART I—SEc.!] 


36. The Authority has examined each programme against the following elements in 
sequence: (i) the legal basis and administering authority; () whether a financial contribution by 
a government or public body is established; (॥) whether the programme is specific; (iv) whether 
a benefit is conferred, and the basis on which the benefit has been measured; and (v) the ad 
valorem subsidy rate. Where any of the first three elements is not established, no rate has been 
determined. 


37. Anmnexures to the Rules. The Authority has determined the amount of the 
countervailable subsidy in accordance with Annexure IV to the Rules, which sets out the 
guidelines for the calculation of the amount of subsidy, and has examined whether each 
programme is a subsidy conferred on a limited number of persons in accordance with Annexure 
II to the Rules read with Article 2 of the SCM Agreement. Injury has been determined in 
accordance with Rule |3 of the Rules read with Annexure I to the Rules. 


38. Recurring and non-recurring benefits. A benefit conferred and consumed within the 
year in which it arises has been treated as recurring and expensed to that year. A benefit 
conferred once but enjoyed over the life of the asset which it finances has been treated as non- 
recurring and allocated over the average useful life of !5 years of the renewable physical assets 
used in the production of the subject goods, only the portion attributable to the period of 
investigation having been countervailed. The Authority has applied that treatment to the 
provision of land and to the exemptions from sales tax on equipment and from import duty on 
machinery. In respect of every other programme the Authority has examined the records of the 
respondent concerned and has determined upon that examination whether the benefit is recurring 
or non-recurring, the classification so determined being recorded at the programme concerned. 
The provision of natural gas and electricity, the exemption of import duty and sales tax on raw 
materials and consumables, and income-tax allowances claimed in the year of assessment falling 
within the period of investigation have been treated as recurring. 


39. Denominator. A subsidy which is not tied to a particular product has been allocated over 
the total sales of the recipient; a subsidy tied to a particular product or facility has been allocated 
over the sales of that product or facility. 


40. Computation of the ad valorem subsidy rate. For every programme the rate has been 
computed as a fraction. The numerator is the amount of the benefit attributable to the period of 
investigation. The denominator is the turnover described in the preceding paragraph. The rate is 
the numerator expressed as a percentage of the denominator. 


Al. The numerator is arrived at as follows. Where the benefit is recurring, the whole of the 
benefit arising in the period of investigation is taken. Where the benefit is non-recurring, the 
benefit is first computed in full and then divided by the average useful life of fifteen years, so 
that only one-fifteenth of it is taken into the period of investigation; the Authority has applied 
that treatment to the provision of land and to the exemptions from sales tax on equipment and 
from import duty on machinery. In respect of the remaining programmes the Authority has 
determined the amount attributable to the period of investigation upon the verified records of the 
respondent concerned, and the treatment adopted is recorded at the programme concerned. 
Where the benefit arises in a currency other than that of the denominator, it is converted into the 
currency of the denominator at the rate used by the respondent in its own questionnaire response, 
so that numerator and denominator stand in the same currency; no rate of the Authority’s own 
has been substituted for a rate the respondent has evidenced.

price. Xinyi Energy Smart (Malaysia) submitted that the relevant land parcels were purchased 
directly from Perbadanan Kemajuan Negeri Melaka through private sales; that it could not locate 
the applicable guideline value; and that it could not confirm whether similar price and payment 
terms were available to other industrial users. 


49. Examination by the Authority — financial contribution. The provision of land 
constitutes a financial contribution only where the land is provided by a government or a public 
body. The Authority has examined the position in respect of each parcel: 


i. In the case of Xinyi Energy Smart (Malaysia), the parcels were acquired from a State 
Development Corporation, which is a public body, and the element is satisfied. 


ii. In the case of Kibing Group (M), one parcel was acquired from a government-linked 
entity and one from a party which the respondent describes as a private entity. A purchase 
from a private vendor does not constitute a financial contribution by the Government of 
Malaysia at any price. The Authority has accordingly excluded that parcel from 
consideration and has examined only the parcel acquired from the government-linked 
entity. 


lii. In the case of Jinjing Technology Malaysia, the leasehold interest was originally allotted 
by a government-owned corporation and passed to the respondent from a cross-owned 
affiliate. The Authority determines that the interposition of a cross-owned affiliate does 
not defeat the finding. The land is land in the subject country, allotted by a body of that 
country, in respect of the very site on which the subject goods are produced, and it has at 
all times since allotment been dedicated to that production. To hold otherwise would 
permit the benefit of a government allotment to be insulated from countervailing 
measures by the routing of title through an affiliate. 


50. The Authority records that this determination is to be distinguished from its 
determination on policy lending recorded below. In the case of policy lending, the loans were

extended by lenders outside the subject country to entities outside the subject country, in respect 
of no asset situated in the subject country, and the subsequent movement of funds between 
affiliates did not convert them into a financial contribution by the Government of Malaysia. In 
the present case the financial contribution was made by a body of the subject country in respect 
of the site of production situated in that country. 


5I. Examination by the Authority — specificity. Land in a designated industrial park is not 
available generally. It is allotted only to enterprises admitted to that park, upon application and 
approval. The programme is accordingly specific within the meaning of Article 2.2 of the SCM 
Agreement, being limited to enterprises located within a designated geographical region, and in 
the alternative under Article 2.l(a), being limited to enterprises approved for admission. 


52. Examination by the Authority — benefit. No guideline value was furnished by any 
respondent, and no respondent has contended that a contemporaneous transaction is available for 
comparison. The Authority has relied upon the Malaysia Industrial Park Directory published by 
the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers in collaboration with the Malaysian Investment 
Development Authority and relevant stakeholders, which provides information on industrial 
parks including the developer, tenure, selling prices and infrastructure available. The Directory 
was prepared as an investor-oriented reference for assessing and identifying suitable industrial 
locations, is independently published and publicly available, and was prepared with the 
participation of the national investment authority. The Authority accordingly considers the 
selling prices reported therein to be relevant and objective publicly available information 
regarding prevailing industrial land prices in Malaysia, and an appropriate and reliable basis for 
determining the applicable benchmark. 


53. The Authority does not accept the contention that a privately negotiated transaction, or 
the absence of a guideline value, establishes that the consideration paid represents prevailing 
market value. A negotiated price between a state corporation and an applicant enterprise is not, 
without more, a market price; the question under Article l4(d) is whether the remuneration was 
adequate by reference to prevailing market conditions, and not whether the parties negotiated. 
The Authority has therefore compared the consideration actually paid or contracted with the 
applicable benchmark rate for the industrial park concerned. 


54. The Authority further notes that, in the case of Xinyi Energy Smart (Malaysia), the 
information furnished by the respondent itself records that certain of the parcels acquired are not 
used for the production of the subject merchandise. A benefit conferred in respect of land which 
does not support production of the subject goods is not attributable to the subject goods, and 
those parcels have accordingly been excluded. 


55. The acquisition of land is a one-time benefit conferred in respect of an asset used over a 
number of years and has accordingly been treated as non-recurring and allocated over the 
average useful life in accordance with the allocation rule set out in the methodology above, only 
the portion attributable to the period of investigation having been countervailed. 


56. Computation of the benefit. The benefit has been computed parcel by parcel. For each 
qualifying parcel the Authority has taken the area in square feet and multiplied it by the 
benchmark rate per square foot for the industrial park in which that parcel stands, so arriving at 
the benchmark value of the parcel; from that value it has deducted the consideration actually paid 
or contracted by the respondent. The benchmark rate applied is RM 35 per square foot in the

case of each of the three parks concerned, being the rate reported for that park in the Malaysia 
Industrial Park Directory; where the Directory reports a range for a park, the lower end of the 
range has been taken. 


57. The numerator is the aggregate of the amounts so computed for the qualifying parcels of 
the respondent, divided by fifteen, being the average useful life adopted in the methodology 
above. In the case of the leasehold interest held by Jinjing Technology Malaysia the Authority 
has allocated the benefit over the average useful life of fifteen years and not over the sixty-year 
term of the lease, the allocation period under Annexure IV being referable to the useful life of the 
asset employed in production and not to the duration of the title by which it is held. The 
denominator is the total turnover of the respondent in the period of investigation, expressed in 
ringgit. Parcels not used for the production of the subject goods, and the parcel acquired from a 
private vendor, have been excluded from the numerator for the reasons already recorded, while 
the denominator remains the whole turnover of the respondent, the benefit not being tied to any 
particular product.

Programme 2: Provision of Natural Gas for Less Than Adequate Remuneration 


59. Views of the Domestic Industry. The Government of Malaysia regulates domestic 
natural gas prices through Government-controlled entities and provides natural gas to industrial 
consumers, including float glass manufacturers, at prices below prevailing market prices. The 
regulated pricing framework enables eligible industrial users to procure natural gas at prices 
lower than international market benchmarks, thereby reducing production costs. The 
Government, through its pricing policy and regulatory framework, provides natural gas for less 
than adequate remuneration within the meaning of Article l4(d) of the SCM Agreement and 
Section 9 of the Act. The gas prices reported by the exporters should not be accepted in the 
absence of reliable and complete information from the Government of Malaysia, mere 
submission of invoice prices not establishing that such prices are representative of undistorted 
market prices, and appropriately adjusted Indonesian natural gas prices should be considered as 
an external benchmark, Indonesia being a geographically proximate and economically 
comparable regional benchmark. 


60. Submissions by the Government and other interested parties. The Government of 
Malaysia and the responding producers/exporters submitted that domestic natural gas prices are 
determined under the applicable statutory and regulatory framework and are not established for 
the benefit of any particular enterprise or industry. The responding producers/exporters 
purchased natural gas at the applicable regulated industrial tariff and did not receive any 


[भाग lars ] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 89 


preferential pricing or additional concession unavailable to other similarly situated industrial 
consumers. Copies of gas purchase agreements, invoices and payment records were furnished. 
The respondents disputed the benchmark proposed by the domestic industry and submitted that 
international LNG prices or export prices are not appropriate benchmarks for determining 
adequacy of remuneration under Article 4(d). 


6l. | Examination by the Authority — financial contribution. Domestic piped natural gas is 
supplied under a regulated framework in which a wholly State-owned corporation is the sole 
aggregator of domestic supply and in which the price payable is fixed under a mechanism 
administered by or on behalf of the Government. The supply of natural gas on those terms 
constitutes the provision of goods by the Government or by a public body within Article 
.l(a)()(@i) of the SCM Agreement and Section 9 of the Act. The Government of Malaysia has 
not disputed the regulated character of the framework. 


62. Examination by the Authority — specificity. The Government of Malaysia has 
submitted that domestic natural gas prices are determined under the applicable statutory and 
regulatory framework and are not established for the benefit of any particular enterprise or 
industry. The question is not whether the framework names the float glass industry. It is whether 
the regulated price is available to enterprises generally, or only to some. The Authority has 
examined the framework on that question and finds the availability limited in two distinct ways. 


63. First, limited by connection and by category. The regulated price is not available to 
any enterprise that wishes to buy gas. It is available only to an enterprise connected to the piped 
distribution network, and only in the area to which the framework extends; and within that 
network it is available only to an enterprise falling within one of the consumer categories 
designated under the applicable instruments, on terms fixed by or on behalf of the Government. 
An enterprise outside the network, or outside a designated category, cannot obtain gas at that 
price at all. A measure so confined is limited to certain enterprises within the meaning of Article 
2.l(a) of the SCM Agreement read with Annexure II to the Rules, and is in the alternative 
limited to enterprises located within a designated geographical region within the meaning of 
Article 2.2. 


64. Secondly, limited in fact by the nature of the benefit. Even upon the assumption that 
the regulated price is nominally open to a wide class, the advantage it confers is not evenly 
spread. The benefit of a price concession on gas accrues in proportion to the gas consumed. The 
manufacture of float glass requires a furnace held continuously at temperature and is among the 
most gas-intensive of industrial activities, and the responding producers/exporters are consumers 
of gas in very substantial quantities. A concession of this character is therefore used by, and is 
predominantly used by, a limited number of enterprises within the meaning of Article 2.l(c), 
whatever the terms of the instrument may say. 


65. The Authority accordingly determines that the programme is specific. The Authority 
records that the first ground rests upon the terms of the framework and the second upon its effect 
in fact, and that either ground is sufficient. 


66. Examination by the Authority — benefit. The Authority has considered whether the 
domestic reference price determined under the Malaysian regulatory framework may serve as the 
benchmark, and has concluded that it may not. That reference price is not a market price. It is the 
administered price fixed under the very framework which is alleged to confer the subsidy, in a 


90 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART I—SEc.!] 


market in which a wholly State-owned corporation is the sole aggregator of domestic supply. 
Where the government is the predominant provider and itself fixes the price, the in-country price 
is determined by the government’s own role in the market and cannot serve as a measure of the 
adequacy of the remuneration which the government receives; to adopt it would be to test the 
measure against itself. 


67. Having concluded that no usable in-country benchmark exists, the Authority has adopted 
an out-of-country benchmark, being the price at which natural gas was available on 
commercial terms in Indonesia outside the administered framework, that being the nearest 
regional market for which prices outside an administered framework are available in the period 
of investigation. The adoption of a regional benchmark of this description was proposed by the 
domestic industry, and Indonesia is geographically proximate and economically comparable to 
the subject country. 


68. The benchmark series applied follows the price which was in fact available in each 
month, the Authority having taken in each month the non-administered price at which gas could 
then be obtained, and not a single annual average. Specifically, for April 2024, the benchmark 
price taken was US$ .89 per MMBtu, corresponding to the non-administered pipeline price for 
the lowest published consumer category. For the period from May 2024 to December 2024, the 
benchmark price was US$ 3.00 per MMBtu based on the regasified liquefied natural gas price. 
Finally, for the period from January 2025 to March 2025, the benchmark price was US$ 6.77 
per MMBtu, reflecting the regasified liquefied natural gas price for that quarter. 


69. Regasified LNG pricing was introduced by the supplier only in May 2024, and for April 
2024 the pipeline price has accordingly been taken. That price is published by consumer 
category; the category applicable to each respondent is not on the record, and the Authority has 
taken the lowest published category, being the level least adverse to the respondents. The price 
of US$ 9.6 per MMBtu appearing on the record has not been adopted, having been superseded 
on 0.0.2023, six months before the period of investigation began. 


70. The Authority has examined the applicable regulatory framework, the gas supply 
agreements, the invoices and payment records, the competing submissions on the appropriate 
benchmark, and the benefit calculations placed on record. 


7l. Computation of the benefit. For each of the twelve months of the period of 
investigation the Authority has taken the quantity of natural gas purchased by the respondent in 
MMBtu and the price in fact paid by it per MMBtu, as appearing from its own invoices, and has 
multiplied the quantity by the amount, if any, by which the benchmark for that month exceeds 
the price paid. Where the benchmark for a month did not exceed the price paid, no benefit has 
been taken for that month. The numerator is the sum of the twelve monthly amounts so 
computed, converted into ringgit at the rate used by the respondent in its own response. The 
denominator is the total turnover of the respondent in the period of investigation in ringgit, the 
benefit not being tied to any particular product. The benefit is recurring and the whole of it has 
been taken into the period of investigation. Quantities invoiced in other units have been 
converted to MMBtu at the conversion factor used by the respondent itself. 


72. Based upon the verified information available on record, the Authority determines that 
natural gas was provided for less than adequate remuneration, that the programme constitutes a

Programme 3: Investment Tax Allowance and Reinvestment Allowance 


73. Views of the Domestic Industry. The Government of Malaysia grants Investment Tax 
Allowance to qualifying manufacturing enterprises undertaking approved investments, 
permitting deduction of a prescribed percentage of qualifying capital expenditure against 
statutory income and thereby reducing the income tax liability of eligible enterprises. The 
programme constitutes government revenue foregone and confers a measurable financial benefit. 


74. Submissions by the Government and other interested parties. The Government of 
Malaysia submitted the relevant provisions governing the Investment Tax Allowance under the 
Promotion of Investments Act, 986, and stated that none of the responding producers/exporters 
received Investment Tax Allowance benefits in relation to the subject goods during the period of 
investigation. Kibing Group (M) submitted that it had claimed benefit under this scheme. Xinyi 
Energy Smart (Malaysia) submitted that it had claimed an ITA-equivalent income-tax exemption 
and a Reinvestment Allowance during 2024 and furnished the relevant tax and approval 
documents. Jinjing Technology Malaysia submitted that it did not benefit from Investment Tax 
Allowance or investment-linked deductions during the period of investigation.

otherwise chargeable constitutes government revenue otherwise due which is foregone within 
Article |.l(a)(l)Gi) of the SCM Agreement and Section 9 of the Act. The Investment Tax 
Allowance is not generally available: it is granted under the Promotion of Investments Act only 
in respect of approved promoted activities and promoted products, upon application to and 
approval by the Malaysian Investment Development Authority. A benefit confined to activities 
and products designated by the Government, and granted upon approval, is specific within the 
meaning of Article 2.l(a) and Article 2.l(c) of the SCM Agreement. The Reinvestment 
Allowance is confined to companies engaged in manufacturing which reinvest in qualifying 
projects and is accordingly limited to a group of industries within Article 2.l(a). The Authority 
notes that the submission of the Government of Malaysia that no benefit was received under 
these programmes is not correct, two of the participating exporters having accepted receipt of 
benefit thereunder, and one of them having disclosed a programme which the Government did 
not disclose at all. The Authority further notes that Jinjing Technology Malaysia held an income- 
tax exemption under the Northern Corridor Economic Region, which is examined as Programme

Programme 4: Industrial Building Allowance and Accelerated Capital Allowance 


79. Views of the Domestic Industry. The Government of Malaysia grants Industrial 
Building Allowance under Schedule 3 of the Income Tax Act 967 in respect of qualifying 
industrial buildings, and Accelerated Capital Allowance permitting accelerated depreciation of 
qualifying capital assets. Both reduce taxable income and constitute government revenue 
foregone. 


80. Submissions by the Government and other interested parties. The Government of 
Malaysia submitted the applicable statutory provisions and stated that none of the responding 
producers/exporters received benefits under either programme in relation to the subject goods 
during the period of investigation. Kibing Group (M) submitted that it had received benefit under

the Industrial Building Allowance. Xinyi Energy Smart (Malaysia) and Jinjing Technology 
Malaysia submitted that they had claimed benefit under the Accelerated Capital Allowance. 


8l. | Examination by the Authority. Both allowances reduce the tax otherwise chargeable 
and constitute revenue foregone within Article |.l(a)(l)(@i) of the SCM Agreement. As regards 
specificity, the Authority notes that neither allowance is available to every taxpayer upon 
incurring expenditure of any description. The Industrial Building Allowance is available only 
in respect of expenditure upon buildings of a description qualifying under the Schedule, that is to 
say buildings used for purposes of manufacture and like activities, and is therefore confined to 
enterprises engaged in those activities. The Accelerated Capital Allowance is not part of the 
general capital allowance regime but is conferred by rules made from time to time in respect of 
designated categories of assets and designated activities, and is available only to enterprises 
which acquire assets of those categories or carry on those activities. Each allowance is 
accordingly limited to certain enterprises within the meaning of Article 2.l(a) of the SCM 
Agreement read with Annexure II to the Rules. The Authority determines that both 
programmes are specific. The Authority has examined the questionnaire responses, tax records 
and verification findings placed on record. 


82. Computation of the benefit. Each of these allowances operates by permitting a 
deduction in respect of qualifying capital expenditure at a rate higher, or at a time earlier, than 
the depreciation otherwise allowable. The benefit is the tax deferred or foregone by reason of the 
accelerated or additional deduction, and the Authority has examined the allowance claimed and 
admitted by each respondent against its tax returns and assessments. In the case of Jinjing 
Technology Malaysia the Authority has satisfied itself that the amount so appearing is the 
allowance multiplied by the rate of corporate income tax applicable to that respondent, and has 
taken that amount as the benefit. In the case of Kibing Group (M) the Authority finds that the 
amount so appearing is the allowance itself; the benefit has accordingly been recomputed as the 
allowance multiplied by the rate of corporate income tax of 24 per cent applicable to that 
respondent, for the reasons stated in relation to the preceding programme. The numerator is the 
amount so determined and the denominator is the total turnover of the respondent in the period of 
investigation. The benefit has been treated as arising in, and confined to, the year of assessment 
in which the allowance was claimed, the deduction being taken in that year; it has accordingly 
not been allocated over the average useful life of the asset to which the expenditure relates, and 
only the amount attributable to the period of investigation has been countervailed.

Programme 5: Sales Tax Exemption on Imported Raw Materials and Equipment 


84. Views of the Domestic Industry. The Government of Malaysia exempts eligible 
manufacturers from payment of sales tax on specified goods, raw materials, components and 
packaging materials. Such exemptions constitute government revenue foregone, reduce the 
production costs of eligible enterprises and confer a measurable financial benefit. 


85. Submissions by the Government and other interested parties. The Government of 
Malaysia submitted that the programme is governed by the Sales Tax (Persons Exempted from 
Payment of Tax) Order 208. Kibing Group (M) submitted that it availed the Schedule C sales 
tax exemption as a registered manufacturer, the exemption applying to raw materials, 
components and packaging used in manufacturing activities. Jinjing Technology Malaysia and 
Xinyi Energy Smart (Malaysia) submitted that they operate under the Licensed Manufacturing 
Warehouse framework and, in respect of sales tax, relied upon a determination of the U.S. 
Department of Commerce to the effect that the benefit of a sales tax exemption accrues to the 
purchaser rather than to the seller. 


86. Examination by the Authority. Exemption from a tax otherwise payable constitutes 
revenue foregone within Article |.l(a)()(ii) of the SCM Agreement. 


87. As regards the reliance placed upon the determination of the U.S. Department of 
Commerce, that determination is on record and has been examined. It contains two distinct 
holdings: first, that in respect of the exemption applicable to the finished product the benefit 
accrues to the purchaser and not to the seller, the producer’s role being limited to remitting a tax 
borne by the buyer; and secondly, that in respect of the exemption applicable to input materials 
the programme was not specific on the record then before that authority. The Authority is not 
bound by the determination of the investigating authority of another Member and considers it 
distinguishable in the present case for the following reasons: 


i. The first holding has no application to the programme in issue. It concerns tax upon the 
producer’s output sales. The exemption examined here is an exemption upon the 
respondent’s inputs and equipment, in respect of which the respondent is itself the 
purchaser and therefore, upon the reasoning of that determination, the party upon which 
the benefit falls. 


ii. That determination was made under the sales tax legislation then in force in Malaysia. The 
regime presently in issue was introduced with effect from 0.09.208 under the Sales Tax 
Act 20I8, and the instrument in issue is Schedule C of the Order made thereunder, which 
operates by application to and approval by the Royal Malaysian Customs Department of 
a registered manufacturer in respect of an approved list of goods. The respondent has 
itself described the exemption as availed “as a registered manufacturer”. A finding of 
non-specificity made upon the earlier legislation does not determine the character of the 
instrument now in issue. 


iii. That determination concerned a different product, a different period of investigation and 
different respondents, and the finding of non-specificity rested expressly upon the 
information which that authority was able to collect and verify upon the record of that 
case.

88. As regards specificity, the Authority determines, for the reasons recorded above in 
relation to the sales tax exemption on raw materials, that the exemption is not available as of 
right to all persons but is granted upon application, registration and approval of a specified 
manufacturer in respect of an approved list of goods, and is accordingly specific within the 
meaning of Article 2.l(a) and Article 2.l(c) of the SCM Agreement. 


89. | Computation of the benefit. The exemption operates upon goods brought in during the 
period of investigation, and the benefit is the sales tax which would have been payable upon 
those goods but for the exemption. The Authority has taken the value of the goods covered by 
the exemption certificates and entered during the period of investigation, as appearing from the 
respondent’s own customs entries and purchase records, and has applied to that value the rate of 
sales tax which would otherwise have been chargeable. The numerator is the amount so 
computed. The denominator is the total turnover of the respondent in the period of investigation. 
In the case of raw materials, consumables and packing materials the benefit is recurring, the 
goods being consumed in the year, and the whole of the amount has been taken into the period of 
investigation. In the case of equipment, the goods being capital assets employed in production 
over a number of years, the benefit is non-recurring and, after considering the post-disclosure

one-fifteenth of it having been taken into the period of investigation. The Authority has 
examined the exemption certificates, customs entries and purchase records relating to both 
components and has satisfied itself as to the amounts so determined. The rate determined upon 
equipment reflects that allocation.
