Programme 6: Exemption from Import Duty on Raw Materials, Machinery and Spare Parts 
9l. Views of the Domestic Industry. The Government of Malaysia grants exemption from 


import duty on imported raw materials, components, machinery, spares and consumables used in 
manufacturing activities. Such exemptions reduce the cost of production and constitute 
government revenue foregone within Article |.l(a)()@i) of the SCM Agreement, and are 
specific to enterprises satisfying the prescribed eligibility conditions. 


92. Submissions by the Government and other interested parties. The Government of 
Malaysia submitted that exemptions from import duty on raw materials and components are 
governed by the Customs Act 967 and related customs notifications. All three participating 
Malaysian producers/exporters submitted that they availed exemption from import duty on raw 
materials, spare parts, accessories and machinery — two of them under the Licensed 
Manufacturing Warehouse scheme established under Section 65A of the Customs Act 967, and 


96 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART I—SEc.]] 


the third under the applicable customs framework. It was further submitted that exemption from 
import GST is merely a creditable indirect tax and therefore does not constitute a subsidy, and, in 
relation to a separate allegation, that exemptions relating to import duty and sales tax on spares, 
machinery, equipment and raw materials arise automatically under the preferential tariff 
treatment available under the India-ASEAN Free Trade Agreement upon submission of the 
prescribed Certificate of Origin, and accordingly do not involve a financial contribution by the 
Government of Malaysia. 


93. | Examination by the Authority. The Authority accepts the contention in relation to 
import GST: a creditable indirect tax which the taxpayer would in any event recover confers no 
benefit, and no amount has been countervailed on that account. The Authority likewise accepts 
the contention in relation to preferential tariff treatment under a free trade agreement: such 
treatment is not a subsidy and no amount has been countervailed on that account. 


94. Exemption from import duty otherwise payable constitutes revenue foregone within 
Article l.l(a)(l)(@i) of the SCM Agreement. A Licensed Manufacturing Warehouse licence is 
granted upon application to and approval by the Royal Malaysian Customs Department, and the 
exemption is available only to licence holders in respect of an approved list of goods. The 
programme is accordingly specific within the meaning of Article 2.l(a) and Article 2.l(c) of 
the SCM Agreement. The Authority notes that in the case of one respondent the import duty 
exempted on raw materials is nil, the applicable tariff upon its raw material imports being zero, 
the benefit arising only upon machinery and spare parts. 


95. Computation of the benefit. The benefit is the import duty which would have been 
payable upon the goods entered under the exemption but for the exemption. The Authority has 
taken the assessable value of the goods entered during the period of investigation under each 
exemption, as appearing from the respondent’s own customs entries, and has applied to that

J. METHODOLOGY FOR INJURY ASSESSMENT 


i2. Rule I3 of the Rules deals with the principles governing the determination of injury and 
provides as follows: 


+]३ Determination of injury.— (J) In the case of imports from specified countries, the 
designated authority shall give a further finding that the import of such article into 
India causes or threatens material injury to any industry established in India, or 
materially retards the establishment of an industry in India. (2) Except when a finding 
of injury is made under sub-rule (3), the designated authority shall determine the 
injury, threat of injury, material retardation to the establishment of an industry and the 
causal link between the subsidized import and the injury, taking into account inter alia, 
the principle laid down in Annexure I to the rule. (3) The designated authority may, in 
exceptional cases, give a finding as to the existence of injury even where a substantial 
portion of the domestic industry is not injured if — (i) there is a concentration of 
subsidized imports into an isolated market, and ता) the subsidized imports are causing 
injury to the producers of almost all of the production within such market.” 


l3. The Authority records that the present determination proceeds upon the basis of present 
material injury. Neither threat of material injury nor material retardation of the establishment of 
an industry is claimed or determined.

4. Rule 6(4)(c) and Rule 6(4)(d) of the Rules require the Authority to terminate an 
investigation immediately, by issue of a public notice, if it determines that the amount of subsidy 
is less than one per cent ad valorem, or in the case of a product originating from a developing 
country the amount of subsidy is less than two per cent; or that the volume of the subsidised 
imports, actual or potential, or the injury where applicable, is negligible, or in the case of a 
product originating in a developing country the volume of the subsidised imports represents less 
than four per cent of the total imports of the like product into India, unless imports from 
developing countries whose individual shares of total imports represent less than four per cent 
collectively account for more than nine per cent of the total imports of the like product into India. 
The said provisions give effect to Article 27.l0(a) and Article 27.l0(b) of the SCM Agreement. 
The obligation is couched in mandatory terms, and where the threshold is attracted no discretion 
survives to continue the investigation in respect of the country concerned.

N. NON-ATTRIBUTION ANALYSIS 


50. Having examined the existence of injury and the volume and price effects of the 
subsidised imports, the Authority has examined whether injury to the domestic industry can be 
attributed to any factor other than the subsidised imports, as listed under the Rules and in 
accordance with Article 5.5 of the SCM Agreement, and has separated and distinguished the 
injurious effects of such other factors. 


N.l Capacity expansion, depreciation and interest cost 


5l. The opposing interested parties have contended that the deterioration in profitability is 
attributable to the domestic industry’s own capacity expansion and to the resulting depreciation 
and interest burden rather than to the subject imports. The domestic industry has answered that 
the expansion was a commercial response to growing demand and cannot by itself explain or 
negate the injury. 


52. Examination by the Authority. The Authority accepts that capacity expansion of the 
order undertaken by the domestic industry will have increased its depreciation and interest 
charges and hence its cost of sales, and that a part of the increase in the cost of sales over the 
injury period is attributable to that expansion and not to the subject imports. To that extent the 
contention is well founded and the effect has not been attributed to the subsidised imports. 


53. The contention nonetheless does not explain the injury suffered. Capacity expansion 
explains rising costs. It does not explain falling prices. Over the injury period the cost of sales 
of the domestic industry rose by 43% while its selling price fell by 7%. A producer facing rising 
costs in an undistorted market would raise its prices, or at the least hold them; the domestic 
industry reduced them, in a growing market, in the face of imports whose landed value declined 
to an index of 65 and which undercut its prices in the range of 30-40% in the period of 
investigation. The divergence between a 43% increase in cost and a 7% reduction in price is 
a price effect of the subsidised imports and is not explained by any internal factor 
advanced. 


54. The Authority further notes that the under-recovery of fixed costs arising from the 
decline in capacity utilisation from 95% to 86% is itself a consequence of the inability of the 
domestic industry to sell its production in the face of the subsidised imports, as evidenced by the 
increase in average inventories to 382% of the base year level in a market in which demand rose 
by 30%. That effect is properly attributed to the subject imports and not to the expansion which 
created the capacity.

56. Volume. Imports from the non-subject sources fell from 87,02] MT in the base year to 
4,785 MT in the period of investigation, and their share of Indian demand from a range of 5— 
0% to a range of 0-5%. The Authority does not describe the movement as a continuous decline:

whole the volume declined, and at less than 5% of demand in the period of investigation it is too 
small a share of the market to have displaced the domestic industry, whose own share of demand 
is many times greater. 


57. Price. The Authority records that the landed value of the non-subject imports remained 
below that of the imports from Malaysia throughout the injury period, and that imports from 
Bangladesh in particular entered the Indian market at a markedly low unit value in the period of 
investigation. The Authority does not treat this comparison of aggregate unit values as 
establishing that the non-subject imports set the price in the Indian market. A unit value 
computed over all entries from a source reflects the mix of thicknesses, qualities and grades 
entered from that source, and the record contains no analysis reconciling the product-mix of any 
non-subject source with that of the subject imports or of the domestic like article. A low 
aggregate unit value is therefore as consistent with a thinner or lower-grade mix of entries as it is 
with a genuinely lower price for goods comparable to those under consideration. 


58. Examination. The price injury found in these final findings does not rest upon a 
comparison between one import source and another. It rests upon the comparison between the 
landed value of the subject imports and the domestic industry’s own selling price and cost of 
sales: undercutting in the range of 30-40% in the period of investigation, a selling price that fell 
7% while the cost of sales rose 43%, and a movement from profit into loss. Imports of less than 
5% of demand cannot explain a price effect of that magnitude across the whole market, and the 
volumes concerned declined over the injury period while the injury deepened. The Authority 
therefore determines that the injury suffered by the domestic industry is not attributable to 
the imports from non-subject sources. The Authority records that it has examined this factor 
upon price as well as upon volume. No interested party has, in its post-disclosure comments, 
placed on record any comparison of the non-subject imports with the domestic like article on a 
like-for-like basis of thickness and grade, or any other material showing that the non-subject 
imports set the price in the Indian market.

declined in a growing market in the same period and in the same direction as the price and 
financial parameters of the Applicants, which is consistent with pressure from a common 
external source and not with displacement within the domestic industry.

O. MAGNITUDE OF INJURY MARGIN 


64. The Authority has determined the non-injurious price for the domestic industry in 
accordance with the principles and the methodology uniformly adopted by the Authority for the 
determination of the non-injurious price. The non-injurious price of the product under 
consideration has been determined by adopting the verified information and data relating to the 
cost of production for the period of investigation. For determining the non-injurious price, the 
best utilisation of the raw materials by the domestic industry over the injury period has been 
considered, and the same treatment has been carried out with the utilities. The best utilisation of 
production capacity over the injury period has been considered. It is ensured that no 
extraordinary or non-recurring expenses are charged to the cost of production. A reasonable 
return (pre-tax @ 22%) on average capital employed, that is average net fixed assets plus 
average working capital, for the product under consideration was allowed as pre-tax profit to 
arrive at the non-injurious price in accordance with the said methodology. 


65. The Authority has considered the contention that inefficiencies and expansion- 
related costs should be excluded in determining the non-injurious price. The contention is

well founded in principle and has been given effect. The principles of best utilisation applied to 
raw materials, utilities and production capacity operate to exclude the inefficiency arising from 
under-utilized capacity, and the exclusion of extraordinary and non-recurring expenses operates 
to exclude one-time expansion costs, so that the non-injurious price is not inflated by the 
domestic industry’s own inefficiency. 


66. The landed price for the cooperating exporters has been determined on the basis of the 
data furnished by the exporters. For all the non-cooperating producers/exporters of Malaysia, the 
Authority has determined the landed price on the basis of facts available. The injury margin is 
the amount by which the non-injurious price exceeds the landed price, expressed as a 
percentage of the landed price. A single weighted average non-injurious price has been applied 
to every producer and exporter of Malaysia. No injury margin has been determined in respect of 
Indonesia, the investigation in respect of that country being terminated.

P.l Submissions made on behalf of the opposing interested parties

i. That anti-subsidy duties on the subject goods will significantly raise production costs for

ul. That higher costs could lead to imports of the ultimate products into India. 


ii. That the impact of the duties is much more than what is indicated by the domestic 
industry. 


P.2 Submissions made on behalf of the Domestic Industry 


68. The submissions of the domestic industry with regard to the Indian industry’s interest are 
as follows: 


i. That in the light of the widening trade deficit it is important to rely more on domestic 
production capacities, and that the imposition of duties would allow conservation of 
foreign exchange favouring the balance of payments account. 


il. That the impact of the imposition of anti-subsidy duty on the subject goods will be 
negligible as compared with the cost of the final product.

ili. That since there are already six players in the market, there would be no monopoly in

iv. That the product under consideration can be imported at fair prices from other sources 
also, and that there would therefore be no adverse impact on users. 


v. That the impact of duties would be minimal in project cost based on the prices prevailing

P.3 Examination by the Authority 


69. The Authority notes that the primary objective of anti-subsidy duty is to remedy the 
injury caused to the domestic industry by subsidisation and to restore conditions of fair 
competition in the Indian market. The imposition of anti-subsidy measures is not designed to 
restrict imports; it follows a determination of subsidisation, injury and the causal link between 
the two, and operates to ensure that imports are available at fair and non-subsidised prices. The 
imposition of duty would not affect the availability of the product. 


70. The Authority issued the initiation notification inviting the views of all interested parties, 
including importers, consumers and others, and prescribed a questionnaire for users and 
consumers to provide relevant information. An Economic Interest Questionnaire was also 
prescribed to allow various stakeholders, including the domestic industry, producers/exporters 
and importers, users and consumers, to furnish pertinent information related to the investigation 
including the possible effect of anti-subsidy duty upon their operations. 


7l. The Authority notes that no importer, user or user association filed a questionnaire 
response or any submission in the present investigation. The contentions so recorded have

75. The Authority has examined the post-disclosure submissions made by the interested

On the status of the responding producers/exporters as cooperating parties 


76. The responding producers/exporters filed their questionnaire responses within the time 
allowed, responded to the clarifications sought, and furnished the records against which their 
responses were examined. They have accordingly been treated as cooperating, and individual 
subsidy margins have been determined for each of them on the basis of their own information. 
Where a programme was referred to by an exporter otherwise than in its programme-wise 
answers, the Authority has examined it on the basis of the records on file. 


On the computation of subsidy margins 


77. The Authority has examined the contentions of the responding exporters that the subsidy 
margins require reconsideration on the basis of the exporters’ own computations. The benefit 
amounts, turnover and other figures adopted in the determination are those which emerged upon 
desk verification of each respondent’s supporting records. Where the verified figure differed 
from the self-reported figure, the verified figure has been preferred. On re-examination, the 
Authority has found that the benefits reported by Kibing Group (M) Sdn. Bhd. under the 
Investment Tax Allowance, the Industrial Building Allowance and the Accelerated Capital 
Allowance represented the gross allowance and not the tax foregone, and that the sales tax 
exemption on equipment, being a capital-linked benefit, had been expensed wholly to the period 
of investigation. These benefits have been recomputed as recorded under Programmes 3, 4 and 5, 
and the subsidy margin of Kibing Group (M) Sdn. Bhd. and the residual subsidy margin for 
Malaysia have been revised accordingly. The revision is downward and arises from the 
respondent’s own submissions. Save as aforesaid, the subsidy margins as determined are 
maintained. 


On the natural gas benchmark 


78. The Authority has considered the submissions that (a) the Authority has not examined 
whether the prices paid by the individual respondents are distorted; (b) observable arm’s-length 
domestic transactions in Malaysia should have been considered before resorting to an out-of- 
country benchmark; (c) the adoption of an Indonesian benchmark is inconsistent with the 
Authority’s finding dated 03.03.2026 in the anti-subsidy investigation concerning imports of 
Textured Tempered Glass from Malaysia; and (d) the source and underlying data for the 
benchmark have not been adequately disclosed. 

79. On point (a), the finding in paragraphs 66 to 68 is not a finding that the individual 
respondent’s transaction was distorted; it is a finding that the Malaysian domestic reference price 
itself — being the administered price fixed under the very framework alleged to confer the 
subsidy, in a market in which a wholly State-owned corporation is the sole aggregator of 
domestic supply — cannot serve as a measure of the adequacy of remuneration. The inquiry

under Article l4(d) is directed to the adequacy of the remuneration, not to the terms of the

82. On point (9), the benchmark prices were drawn from the published tariff schedules and

83. As regards the submission that the Indonesian benchmark should be subject to

On the provision of land at LTAR

86. On the allocation period, the benefit has been allocated over fifteen years under Annexure 
IV, the allocation period being referable to the useful life of the asset employed in production 
and not to the duration of the title. As regards the Aluminium Primary Foundry Alloy Ingot

On the exchange rate

On the allocation period for import duty exemption on machinery and spare parts 


88. Having examined the respondents’ submissions, the Authority notes that the exemption 
from import duty on machinery relates to capital assets employed in production over a number of 
years, and is accordingly a non-recurring benefit. Consistently with the methodology recorded in 
Section G and with the treatment of the exemption on equipment in the case of Kibing Group 
(M) Sdn. Bhd., the benefit has been allocated over the average useful life of fifteen years. The 
allocation period of twelve years proposed by the respondents is accordingly not adopted. 


On related and cross-owned entities 


89. Subsidies received by a cross-owned entity are attributable to a respondent only where 
that entity supplies an input primarily dedicated to the production of the subject goods, or is a 
holding company or a producer of the subject goods, and has itself received a financial 
contribution from the Government of Malaysia. The Authority has applied that test to each entity 
named by the domestic industry. Jinjing: its own records, including its income-tax return, 
disclose no purchase of inputs from any related entity in Malaysia, and its related-party 
transactions are with entities outside Malaysia or with private entities, none of which involves a 
financial contribution by the Government of Malaysia. Xinyi: Xinyi has disclosed purchases of a 
material from a related entity and transportation services from Xin Yun Logistics (Malaysia) 
Sdn. Bhd.; transportation services are not an input into the subject goods, and no programme has 
been identified under which the related supplier received a financial contribution in respect of the 
material supplied. Other entities named: as regards Xinyi Photovoltaic (Malaysia) Co., Ltd., CS 
Eco Glass (M) Sdn. Bhd. and Malaysia Kibing Energy Saving Glass Co., Ltd., no material has 
been placed on record showing that any of them supplied an input to the respondent concerned in 
the period of investigation or received a financial contribution from the Government of Malaysia 
attributable to the subject goods. The contention that the responses be rejected in their entirety is 
accordingly not accepted. The concern that all benefits be examined is accepted; the exemption 
held by Jinjing has been examined as Programme 7. 


On Jinjing’s income-tax exemption and U.S. Commerce findings 


90. Jinjing’s income-tax exemption. The contention of the domestic industry has been 
examined. Jinjing’s own records establish that it held an exemption of l00 per cent of its 
statutory income under the Northern Corridor Economic Region during the period of 
investigation, and the programme has been examined as Programme 7. Jinjing itself referred to 
the exemption in its questionnaire response and explained that no benefit had been received 
under it. Its tax computation for the year of assessment falling within the period of investigation 
shows that no statutory income was exempted and no tax was foregone. For the reasons recorded 
at Programme 7, no amount has been countervailed under it.

9!. U.S. Commerce findings. The U.S. Department of Commerce identified Jinjing Silicon 
Technology Sdn. Bhd. and Xin Yun Logistics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd. as cross-owned with Jinjing 
and Xinyi respectively. The Authority has examined whether these entities supplied inputs to the

no transaction with Jinjing Silicon Technology Sdn. Bhd. Xin Yun Logistics provides

upon a different period and record, and establishes cross-ownership but not the supply of any

On non-submission of programme-wise information by the Government of Malaysia 


92. The Authority has assessed the relevant programmes on the basis of the information and 
explanations available on record. Where information was not furnished, the Authority has 
proceeded on the basis of facts available in accordance with the Rules. 


On the import data from Bangladesh 


93. The share of imports from Bangladesh has been determined from the transaction-wise 
import data of DG Systems for the product under consideration, being 9,482 MT out of total 
imports of 3,78,226 MT, or 5.5] per cent. The figure in the application was an estimate made at 
the stage of initiation on the information then reasonably available; the domestic industry has not 
placed on record any transaction-level data establishing a different volume, and the primary data 
prevail. The provisional assessment pursuant to the order of the Hon’ble Delhi High Court 
affects the duty liability on those imports, not the fact or the volume of their import for home 
consumption, and they are accordingly counted in total imports. The contention is examined and 
not accepted. 


On the Minimum Import Price notification 


94. The MIP is a trade-policy measure issued under the Foreign Trade (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 992, distinct in legal basis, purpose, duration and administering authority from 
a countervailing duty under Section 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, 975. The two measures 
operate independently. The injury determination and subsidy margins have been established 
upon verified data for the period of investigation. The MIP, having been notified after the period 
of investigation, does not affect the determination of subsidisation or injury. The existence of a 
separate trade-policy measure of limited duration does not remove the need for a measure to 
offset the subsidisation and injury found where subsidisation, injury and causal link have been 
established. 


95. The submission that the duty should take the form of a reference price is not accepted. 
The ad valorem form is consistently adopted by the Authority in countervailing duty proceedings 
and is appropriate in the present case.

On material injury and causal link 


96. The Authority confirms material injury to the domestic industry on account of subsidised 
imports from Malaysia, as determined on the basis of verified import data, price effects, injury 
parameters and other relevant factors on record. 


On the termination of the investigation in respect of Indonesia 


97. The volume of imports from Indonesia is below the four per cent threshold in the period 
of investigation and in each year of the injury period. The collective share of developing 
countries individually below four per cent is below nine per cent. No interested party placed 
evidence of potential volume above the threshold on the record. The termination under Rule 
6()(d) is confirmed. No subsidy margin, injury margin or countervailing duty is determined or 
recommended in respect of Indonesia, and no programme-wise finding has been made. The 
Indonesian respondent’s rights concerning the alleged programmes are noted as reserved. 


R. CONCLUSION 


98. Having regard to the contentions raised, information provided, and submissions made by 
the interested parties and facts available before the Authority, as recorded in the above finding, 
and on the basis of above analysis of the subsidisation, injury and causal link to the domestic 
industry, the Authority concludes as follows: 
i. The Applicants constitute the domestic industry within the meaning of Rule 2(b) of 
the Rules and the application satisfies the criteria of standing. 


ii. The product under consideration is Clear Float Glass of nominal thickness 4 mm to 
2 mm as per BIS 4900:2000, and the subject goods produced by the domestic 
industry are a like article thereto. 


iii. Indonesia and Malaysia are each a developing country for the purposes of Rule 
6() of the Rules. The volume of the subsidised imports from Indonesia was 
3.40% of the total imports of the like article into India in the period of 
investigation, which is below the threshold of four per cent, and the collective share 
of all developing countries individually below four per cent is 5.897%, which is 
below the threshold of nine per cent. The investigation in respect of Indonesia is 
accordingly terminated under Rule !6(.)(d), and no subsidy margin, injury margin 
or duty is recommended in respect of that country. 


iv. The volume of imports from Malaysia is above the threshold prescribed under Rule 
6()(d), and the investigation continues in respect of that country. 


v.  Countervailable subsidies were availed by the participating producers and exporters 
of Malaysia during the period of investigation, the subsidy margins determined 
being .6% (range l0—20%) in respect of Xinyi Energy Smart (Malaysia) Sdn. 
Bhd., .44% (range l0—20%) in respect of Kibing Group (M) Sdn. Bhd. and 
8.58% (range 0-l0%) in respect of Jinjing Technology Malaysia Sdn. Bhd., with a 
residual margin of 5.66% (range 0—20%) for Malaysia

vi. The domestic industry has suffered injury during the period of investigation in the 
form of significant price undercutting, price depression and price suppression. The 
injury so suffered is material, being reflected in losses, cash losses, negative return 
on investment, accumulation of inventories and declining capacity utilisation. 


vii. The injury margins determined in respect of the producers and exporters of 
Malaysia are as set out in Section O above, and in every case the subsidy margin is 
lower than the injury margin, so that the duty recommended upon application of the 
lesser duty rule is equal to the subsidy margin. 


viii. The material injury suffered by the domestic industry has been caused by the 
subsidised imports of the subject goods from Malaysia. The injurious effects of the 
other known factors, in particular the effect of the capacity expansion of the 
domestic industry upon its cost of sales, have been separated and distinguished and 
have not been attributed to the subsidised imports. 


ix. The Authority is satisfied that the imposition of a definitive countervailing duty on 
imports of the subject goods originating in or exported from Malaysia is warranted 
to offset the subsidisation and the injury caused thereby, in the form and manner set 
out in Section S below. 


S. RECOMMENDATIONS 


99. The Authority notes that the investigation was initiated and notified to all interested 
parties including Government of Malaysia and adequate opportunity was given to provide 
information/evidence on the aspect of subsidization, injury and causal links in favour or against 
thereof. Having initiated and conducted the investigation into subsidization, injury and causal 
links in terms of the Rules laid down and having established positive subsidy margin as well as 
material injury to the domestic industry caused by such subsidized imports, the Authority is of 
the view that imposition of definitive countervailing duty is required to offset subsidization and 
injury. Therefore, the Authority considers it necessary to recommend imposition of definitive 
countervailing duty on the imports of the subject goods from Malaysia in the form and manner 
described hereunder. 


200. In accordance with Rule l9 of the Rules, and having regard to the lesser duty rule 
followed, the Designated Authority hereby recommends the imposition of an anti-subsidy duty 
equal to the lesser of the margin of subsidy and the margin of injury on all imports of the subject 
goods originating in or exported from Malaysia so as to eliminate the material injury caused to 
the domestic industry. 


Accordingly, under the powers conferred by the aforementioned provision, the Authority 
considers it necessary to recommend, and does hereby recommend, the imposition of a definitive 
anti-subsidy duty on the imports of the subject goods from Malaysia for a period of five (5) years 
from the date of publication of the official notification by the Central Government, at the rates 
specified in Column 7 of the duty table appended below

i, क्षति की जांच समग्र रूप से घरेलू उद्योग के लिए किया जाना अपेक्षित है, और भारतीय बाजार का

i. नेपाल से निर्यात उचित और प्रतिस्पर्धी मूल्यों पर किए जाते हैं और घरेलू उद्योग को क्षति नहीं पहुंचा

ii, आवेदक समग्र बाजार मांग और आपूर्ति की स्थितियों के संदर्भ में आयात प्रवृत्तियों की जांच करने में 
विफल रहे हैं, और मूल्य प्रभावों का आकलन विनिर्देशों, गुणवत्ता और बाजार खंडों में अंतर को ध्यान में 
रखते हुए समान-से-समान तुलना पर आधारित नहीं है। 

iv. क्षति विश्लेषण समेकित और सूचकांकित आंकड़ों पर आधारित है जिनका हितबद्ध पक्षकारों द्वारा स्वतंत्र

बांग्लादेश सरकार ने निर्यात सब्सिडी प्रतिशत में वृद्धि की, जिससे बांग्लादेशी निर्यातकों को उपलब्ध 
लागत लाभ में और वृद्धि हुई।

संबंध की जांच आरंभ और संचालित करने के उपरांत, तथा यह स्थापित करने के उपरांत कि विषयगत देशों में 
विषयगत वस्तुओं के उत्पादकों/निर्यातकों ने अधिनियम की धारा 9 के अर्थ के अंतर्गत प्रतिकार योग्य सब्सिडी 
प्राप्त की है, कि घरेलू उद्योग को तात्विक क्षति हुई है और कि यह क्षति सब्सिडी प्राप्त आयातों के कारण हुई है, 
प्राधिकारी का मत है कि सब्सिडीकरण और क्षति की भरपाई के लिए निश्चित प्रतिकारी शुल्क का अधिरोपण 
आवश्यक है। 

499. प्राधिकारी द्वारा अपनाए गए न्यूनतर शुल्क नियम को ध्यान में रखते हुए, प्राधिकारी घरेलू उद्योग को 
हुई क्षति को दूर करने के लिए सब्सिडी मार्जिन और क्षति मार्जिन में से जो कम हो, उसके बराबर निश्चित 
प्रतिकारी शुल्क के अधिरोपण की सिफारिश करता है। प्रत्येक विषयगत देश के नमूने में चयनित प्रत्येक

राशि कॉलम (9) में दर्शाई गई है।

Subject: Countervailing Duty investigation concerning imports of "Jute Products" 
originating in or exported from Bangladesh and Nepal 


No. 6/35/2025-DGTR.— In terms of the Customs Tariff Act, 975, as amended from time to 
time, and the Customs Tariff (Identification, Assessment and Collection of Countervailing Duty 
on Subsidised Articles and for Determination of Injury) Rules, !995, as amended from time to 
time, the Designated Authority hereby records its final findings in the subject investigation. 


A. BACKGROUND OF THE CASE 


. M/s Indian Jute Mills Association (IMMA) and M/s A.P. Mesta Twine Mills Association (AJMA) 


(hereinafter referred to as the "applicants" or "applicant associations") filed an application before 
the Designated Authority (hereinafter referred to as the "Authority") on behalf of the domestic 
industry, in accordance with Section 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, !975, as amended from time 
to time (hereinafter referred to as the "Act"), read with the Customs Tariff (Identification, 
Assessment and Collection of Countervailing Duty on Subsidised Articles and for Determination 
of Injury) Rules, 995, as amended from time to time (hereinafter referred to as the "Rules" or 
"CVD Rules"), for initiation of an anti-subsidy/countervailing duty investigation concerning 
imports of "Jute Products" (hereinafter referred to as the "subject goods" or "product under 
consideration" or "PUC") originating in or exported from Bangladesh and Nepal (hereinafter 
referred to as the "subject countries"). 


. In terms of Article 3.l of the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (ASCM) 
read with Rule 6A of the Rules, the Government of Bangladesh and the Government of Nepal 
were invited for consultations prior to initiation, by scheduling a consultation meeting on Ist 
September 2025. The Government of Nepal did not respond to the invitation. The Government 
of Bangladesh, vide email dated 29th August 2025, sought additional time of sixty days to 
prepare for the consultations. In the absence of any evidence regarding non-countervailability of 
the alleged programmes at that stage, the Authority proceeded on the basis that the existence of 
the alleged programmes and the quantification of the countervailable subsidies were required to 
be analysed through an investigation, while keeping the opportunity of consultations open 
during the course of the investigation. 


. The Authority, on the basis of sufficient prima facie evidence submitted by the applicants, 
issued a public notice vide Notification No. 6/35/2025-DGTR dated 29th September 2025, 
published in the Gazette of India, initiating the subject investigation in accordance with the

C.3 Examination by the Authority 


The product under consideration, as defined in the initiation notification, is "Jute products" 
comprising of jute yarn/twine (single, multiple folded, or cabled), jute sacking bags and cloth, 
and jute hessian bags and fabrics. The scope of the product under consideration also covers the 
subject goods when imported as jute products containing mineral oil or vegetable oil, and as 
"diversified jute product" as defined by the Government of Bangladesh under Article 2(9) of the 
Jute Act, 20l7. The product scope specifically excludes blanket, decorative fabrics, floor 
coverings, hand and shopping bags, handicrafts, carpet backing cloth, geo-textiles and other gift 
novelty items. 


The product under consideration is classifiable under Chapters 53 and 63 of the Customs Tariff 
Act, 975 under headings 5307, 530 and 6305, jute twine also being classifiable under heading 
5607. The customs classifications are indicative only and are in no way binding on the scope of 
the present investigation. 


As regards the contention of the producers/exporters from Nepal, the Authority notes that the 
reference to "diversified jute product" as defined under Article 2(9) of the Bangladesh Jute Act, 
207 is a clarificatory description intended to capture the forms and descriptions under which 
the subject goods are imported from Bangladesh, having regard to the categorisation adopted by 
the Government of Bangladesh for its own fiscal and regulatory purposes. The said reference 
does not enlarge the scope of the product under consideration beyond jute yarn/twine, jute 
sacking bags and cloth, and jute hessian bags and fabrics, and does not impose any obligation 
upon the producers/exporters from Nepal under the laws of Bangladesh. The goods expressly 
excluded under the initiation notification, including carpet backing cloth and geo-textiles, 
remain excluded irrespective of their treatment under the laws of Bangladesh. The apprehension 
of the producers/exporters from Nepal is therefore misplaced. 


As regards the PCN methodology, the Authority notes that the PCN methodology notified in the 
mid-term review investigation No. 7/l/2024-DGTR, in respect of jute yarn/twine, has been 
adopted for the present investigation, and the interested parties have filed their information 
accordingly.

F.3.2 Double remedy 


The Authority notes that Section 9B(l)(a) of the Act does not bar the initiation or conduct of a 
countervailing duty investigation in respect of goods which are subject to anti-dumping duty. 
The provision addresses the manner of imposition of duties, so as to ensure that no article is 
subjected to both countervailing duty and anti-dumping duty to compensate for the same 
situation of dumping or export subsidisation. The subsidy determination in the present 
investigation has been made independently, on the basis of the information relating to the 
subsidy programmes, and is distinct from the determination of dumping in the mid-term review. 
Of the programmes countervailed herein, Programme 8 of the Government of Bangladesh and 
Programme | of the Government of Nepal are contingent upon export performance and operate 
upon the export price of the subject goods; Programme |0 of Bangladesh and Programme 2 of 
Nepal are not contingent upon export performance and are not remedied by the anti-dumping 
duty. The anti-dumping duty on the subject goods, under Notification No. 33/2022-Customs 
(ADD) dated 30th December 2022 and as recommended for re-quantification in the mid-term 
review for the same period of investigation, is expressed as a fixed amount per metric tonne by 
producer and product type. The Authority has accordingly determined the countervailing duty 
for each producer/exporter in two components, the component attributable to the export 
contingent programme and the component attributable to the tax concession, and has considered 
it appropriate, in order to ensure that the same situation of export subsidisation is not 
compensated twice, that the anti-dumping duty continue to be collected in full and that the 
export subsidy component of the countervailing duty be collected only to the extent that it 
exceeds the anti-dumping duty leviable on the same consignment, the tax concession component 
being collected in full. The manner in which this is to be given effect is given below in the 
recommendation.

F.3.3 Claims based on the status of the subject countries as least developed countries. 


The Authority notes that the exemption of least developed country members from the 
prohibition of Article 3.l(a) of the ASCM under Article 27.2(a) operates in respect of the 
prohibition and the remedies under Part वी of the ASCM. It does not immunise subsidised 
imports from countervailing action under Part V of the ASCM and Section 9 of the Act, where 
the subsidies are otherwise countervailable and are causing injury to the domestic industry. 
Article 27.l0 of the ASCM provides, in respect of developing country members, higher de 
minimis and negligibility thresholds for the purposes of countervailing duty investigations. The 
imports from each of the subject countries are individually far above the negligibility threshold, 
and the subsidy margins determined for the sampled producers/exporters, is above the applicable 
de minimis level. The question whether Bangladesh or Nepal has attained export 
competitiveness under Article 27.6 is accordingly not determinative of the maintainability of the 
present countervailing action, and the request for termination on this ground is not acceded to. 


F.3.4 Sampling 


The submissions on sampling were examined by the Authority at the time of confirmation of the 
sample vide notice dated l0th February 2026. The Authority reiterates that although the Anti- 
subsidy Rules do not expressly provide for sampling in an original countervailing duty 
investigation, Rule 23A(3) of the Rules recognises, by necessary implication, a situation in 
which original countervailing duties are determined for a limited set of producers/exporters, and 
cooperative producers/exporters not originally investigated are extended the duty determined for 
the examined producers. A countervailing duty investigation is scheme-centric and evidentiary- 
intensive, involving examination of the existence, nature and specificity of subsidy programmes, 
government measures, financial contributions, benefit and allocation. Individual examination of 
all cooperating producers/exporters would not have been feasible within the statutory time 
limits. 


The Authority limited detailed examination to the producers/exporters accounting for the largest 

representative share of exports, selected three groups from Bangladesh and two groups from 
Nepal, invited and considered comments of the interested parties, and confirmed the sample. 
The selection of producers attracting nil anti-dumping duty ensures that the data examined is 
unaffected by the imposition of anti-dumping duties and provides a reliable basis for assessing 
subsidisation. Non-sampled cooperating producers/exporters are not denied due process, as they 
are accorded a duty based on the sampled producers, which would have been absent had 
complete responses not been filed. 


The request of the producers/exporters from Nepal for individual margins for all five

reasons. The request of the producers/exporters from Bangladesh that the Authority retain 
flexibility to replace a sampled producer/exporter in the event of withdrawal or non-cooperation 
is noted; no such occasion has arisen.

amount of the grant. The incentive is contingent in law upon export performance and is therefore 
deemed to be specific; the Government of Bangladesh has itself acknowledged the export-

The contention of the producers/exporters that the programme is a horizontal export promotion 
measure and hence not specific is misconceived: a subsidy contingent in law upon export 
performance is deemed to be specific, and the availability of export-contingent cash incentives 
to several product sectors does not detract from such deemed specificity. The contention in 
rejoinder that the domestic industry has not demonstrated any identifiable receipt, nexus or 
allocation is inapposite: the benefit has been determined on the cash incentive amounts reported 
and reconciled in the questionnaire responses and supplementary replies of the sampled 
producers/exporters themselves, in respect of their own exports of the subject goods to India 
during the period of investigation. 


The sampled producers/exporters claimed and accrued the incentive on their shipments to India 
at the rates applicable to diversified jute products, on the footing that their products contain at 
least 50% jute by value in terms of the Jute Act, 20l7. The programme being recurring and

exports made during the period of investigation, the sampled producers/exporters having 
themselves submitted that the accrual basis is appropriate, net of the bank charges deducted at 
disbursement as claimed. On this basis, and on the FOB denominator, the Programme 8 margin

Programme l0: Under SRO No. 304-Law/Income Tax-l8/2023, the rate of income tax on 
income from jute products is fixed at 0% for the tax years 2023-24 to 2025-26, as against the 
standard rate of 27.5% applicable to a private limited manufacturing company under the Income

under Section 23 of the said Act operates as the final discharge of tax on export income, and 
tax deducted at source at !0% on disbursement of the cash incentive operates as the final 
discharge of tax on such receipts. The revenue so foregone is a financial contribution within the 
meaning of Section 9 of the Act and Article |.l(a)(l)(@i) of the ASCM, and the concession, 
being limited by law to the jute industry, is specific. The contention that the rate is a uniform 
statutory rate applicable to the entire jute sector and not export contingent does not hold merit: a

within the sector and irrespective of export contingency. The contention of the sampled 
producers/exporters that no benefit arises because !0% is the rate applicable to them assumes 
the very concession under examination and is rejected. 


The sampled producers/exporters have contended, in their comments on the disclosure 
statement, that the cash incentive received under Programme 8 has been countervailed in full 
and gross of the tax deducted at source thereon, and that the tax saving on the same cash 
incentive income cannot thereafter be countervailed again under Programme 40 without 
countervailing the same economic benefit twice. The Authority has examined the contention. 
Under Programme 8 the cash incentive has been countervailed at the full amount of the 
entitlement accruing on exports made during the period of investigation, without deduction of 
the tax deducted at source on it. The tax concession measured on the cash incentive income 
stream under Programme l0 in the disclosure statement was the difference between tax at the 
benchmark rate of 27.5% and tax actually borne on that same amount. Where the incentive has 
been countervailed gross of tax, the tax which the recipient would have borne on it at the 
benchmark rate is already comprised in the amount countervailed, and to measure the

Schedule 2 goods is 50% or more the subsidy is payable at the Schedule | rate of 5%. The 
incentive is disbursed through the exporters commercial bank from a dedicated account 
maintained at the Nepal Rastra Bank and funded in advance by the Ministry of Finance. The

credited, neither reserving prospective operation nor providing for payment or cancellation of 
past claims. No instrument renouncing, cancelling or writing off the accrued entitlements has

H.7 Causal link and non-attribution 

The Authority has examined whether the material injury to the domestic industry has been caused 
by the subsidised imports, and has also examined the other known factors listed in the Rules so as 
to ensure that injury caused by such other factors is not attributed to the subsidised imports. The 
following is noted in this regard: 


a. Volume and prices of imports from third countries 


The imports from the subject countries have accounted for almost the entirety of imports, across 
the injury period. In view of the negligible volume of imports from other countries, such imports 
have not caused injury faced by the domestic industry, and are not likely to cause injury to the 
domestic industry. 


b. Contraction in demand 


. Demand for the product under consideration increased up to 2023-24 and declined by 20% in the 
period of investigation as compared to the preceding year, while remaining at about the level of 
the base year. The Authority has considered whether the contraction in demand accounts for the 
injury to the domestic industry. The decline in absolute volumes in the period of investigation 
was experienced by all participants in the market, the domestic sales of the domestic industry, 
the sales of other Indian producers and the subject imports all being lower than in the preceding 
year, and to that extent the contraction in demand explains part of the decline in the absolute 
volume of production and sales of the domestic industry in the period of investigation. Over the 
injury period as a whole, however, the market share of the subject imports increased from 0% 
to 5% while that of the Indian producers collectively declined by 5 percentage points, and this 
displacement occurred with anti-dumping duty in force and with the Indian industry holding 
capacity to meet the entire demand. Further, the injury to the domestic industry in the period of 
investigation is reflected principally in the price parameters, the landed price of the subject 
imports declined by 20% over the injury period and remained below both the cost of sales and 
the selling price of the domestic industry throughout, and the domestic industry was able to hold 
its volumes in the period of investigation only at the cost of its price realisation, its profit per 
unit declining by 35% over the injury period. The contraction in demand does not explain the 
price undercutting, price suppression and decline in profitability so recorded. The Authority 
therefore notes that, while the contraction in demand has contributed to the decline in absolute 
volumes in the period of investigation, it does not account for the injury caused by the 
subsidised imports through their volume share and price effects, and demand continues to 
remain significant. 


c. Changes in pattern of consumption 


The pattern of consumption with regard to the product under consideration has also not 
undergone any change. Therefore, the domestic industry has not suffered and is not likely to 
suffer injury on this account. 


d. Conditions of competition and trade restrictive practices 


There are no trade restrictive practices or conditions of competition, which may have caused or 
are likely to cause injury to the domestic industry. 


e. Developments in technology 


. Technology for production of the product has not undergone any change and no likely change in 
foreseeable future has been identified by interested parties.

increase in imports in absolute terms and in relation to production and consumption, 
despite existing ADD in place. 

ii. The increase in subsidised imports prevented the domestic industry from selling its goods

ili. As a result of subject imports, the market share of the domestic industry and domestic

J.3. Examination by the Authority 


The Authority recognises that the imposition of countervailing duty might affect the price level of 
the product in India. However, fair competition in the Indian market will not be reduced by the 
imposition of countervailing measures. On the contrary, imposition of the countervailing 
measures would remove the unfair advantage gained by the subsidised imports, prevent the 
decline of the domestic industry and help maintain availability of wider choice to the consumers 
of the subject goods. 


The producers/exporters from Bangladesh have submitted that the public interest analysis of the 
applicants is selective and incomplete, that the impact of the proposed measures on downstream 
industries, consumers, supply availability, competition and prices has not been examined, and 
that no balancing exercise has been undertaken. While offering this comment, these parties have 
not provided relevant information and their analysis on these parameters. The Authority notes 
that the interested parties, including importers, users and their associations, were given adequate 
opportunity to participate and to place on record information on the impact of the proposed duty. 
However, no importer or user has participated to oppose the imposition of the duty or to furnish 
any evidence of possible adverse downstream impact. The domestic industry holds substantial 
unutilised capacity, capacity utilisation being merely 63% in the period of investigation, and 
continuity of supply is not in doubt. The purpose of the duty is to remove the unfair advantage 
conferred by countervailable subsidies, and fair competition in the market would be restored 
rather than reduced.

K.3.l. Programme 8 and Programme 0 of Bangladesh: alleged double counting 


The producers/exporters from Bangladesh have contended that the cash incentive countervailed 
under Programme 8 has again been used as the base for the determination of benefit under 
Programme l0, and that the same benefit has thereby been countervailed twice. The Authority 
has examined the contention. Under Programme 8 the cash incentive has been countervailed at 
the full amount of the entitlement accruing on exports made during the period of investigation, 
gross of the tax deducted at source on it. The benefit determined in the disclosure statement under 
Programme |0 on the cash incentive income stream was the difference between tax at 27.5% and 
the tax actually borne on the same amount. The two programmes are distinct, rest on different 
legal instruments and involve different forms of financial contribution, and the Authority does 
not accept that the tax treatment of a subsidy is in general to be taken into account in measuring 
it. The position of the cash incentive income stream is, however, particular. The amount 
countervailed under Programme 8 already comprises the whole of the incentive, including the 
portion which the recipient would have borne as tax at the benchmark rate, and the concession 
measured on that stream under Programme |0 is that very portion. To countervail it under both 
programmes would measure the same revenue twice. The Authority has therefore accepted the 
contention to this extent and has excluded the cash incentive income stream from the 
determination of benefit under Programme 0, as recorded in Section G.6.l above. The benefit 
under Programme 0 has been re-determined for each sampled entity on the export income and 
domestic income streams alone, by one and the same method for all the sampled entities, and the 
revised determinations are set out in Sections G.7 and G. above. 


The illustration furnished by the producers/exporters, that on an incentive of l00 an amount of 
7.50 is countervailed, proceeds on the premise that the tax treatment of a subsidy must be taken 
into account in measuring it. The Rules provide otherwise. In terms of Rule |2 of the Rules read 
with Annexure IV thereto, a direct transfer of funds is measured at the amount received by the 
recipient and a tax reduction is measured as the difference between the tax actually paid and the 
tax payable at the normal rate, and no allowance can be made for any tax effects of subsidies. 
Each of the two subsidies has been determined in accordance with these provisions, and the 
countervailing duty recommended does not exceed the amount of subsidy so determined, as 
required by Section 9() of the Act, Rule 20 of the Rules and Article 9.4 of the ASCM. The cash 
incentive income stream has accordingly been retained in the determination of benefit under 
Programme |0, as disclosed. 


The Authority does not accept the further contention of A. M. Jute Industries Limited that no 
benefit at all should be quantified under Programme |0. The reduced rate of !0% on the income 
of the jute industry, and the treatment of the tax collected or deducted at source as the final 
discharge of tax on export income, are revenue foregone by the Government of Bangladesh on 
the export income and domestic income of the recipient, which is income independent of the cash 
incentive, and confer a benefit equal to the tax that would otherwise have been payable at the 
standard rate on that income. The exclusion of the cash incentive income stream does not extend 
to those streams. The producers/exporters have themselves accepted in their comments that 
Programme l0 need not be disregarded altogether.

further been submitted that the subsidy margins have been disclosed in ranges, which obscures 
the true picture; that the evidence of injury and causal link is insufficient in terms of Article l.2 
of the ASCM, the share of imports from Bangladesh having remained broadly constant and the 
economic parameters of the domestic industry showing improvement; that the landed value, the 


90 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART I—SEc. !] 


price undercutting and the injury margin have been computed without adding the anti-dumping 
duty in force; that the non-injurious price has been kept confidential; that the same injury, over 
the same injury period and period of investigation, has already been attributed to dumped 
imports in the mid-term review; that the anti-dumping duty in force already neutralises the effect 
of the export subsidy reflected in the export price, so that the levy of countervailing duty would 
amount to a double remedy contrary to Article VI:5 of GATT 994, Article 9.3 of the ASCM 
and Section 9B(l) of the Act; that the non-confidential version of the application does not 
contain meaningful summaries as required under Article 2.4.] of the ASCM; that Cheviot 
Company Ltd. is an importer of the subject goods and that, upon its exclusion, the remaining 
applicants may account for less than 25% of Indian production; that the non-consideration of its 
response and post-hearing submissions in the disclosure statement is inconsistent with Articles 
2.] and 2.7 of the ASCM; and that the investigation should be terminated in terms of Article 
.9 of the ASCM. 


95. The Authority has examined the submissions. As recorded in the relevant section above, 
the response and the submissions of the Government of Bangladesh have been taken on record 
and considered. As regards Programmes | to 7, 9, |] and 2, no benefit has been determined for 
any of the sampled producers/exporters and no duty has been recommended on account of these 
programmes, and the submissions do not call for any further finding. As regards Programme 8, 
the Government of Bangladesh has itself described the programme as an export incentive 
maintained in terms of Article 27 of the ASCM, the incentive is payable on the export of jute 
goods at the rates notified in the circulars of Bangladesh Bank, and the rates of 0%, 5% and 3% 
stated by the Government of Bangladesh for 2024-25 correspond to FE Circular No. |2 dated 
30.06.2024, which has been applied by the Authority for exports made from Ist July 2024. A 
programme under which payment is made upon export is contingent upon export performance, 
and the availability of the incentive to other export sectors does not alter this position. The claim 
based on the status of Bangladesh as a least developed country has been dealt with in the 
relevant section above. The benefit has been determined on the basis of the amounts reported by 
the sampled producers/exporters, and the reduction in the rates is reflected therein. Any change 
in the programme after the period of investigation is a matter which can be examined in a review 
under the Rules. As regards Programme 0, the response confirms that the reduced rate under 
SRO No. 304 is available only on income derived from the manufacture of jute goods. A benefit 
limited by law to an industry is specific, and the uniform application of the rate within that 
industry does not make it non-specific. The submission that the programme is not contingent 
upon export performance is consistent with the treatment of the programme by the Authority. 
The contention that there is no profit and hence no benefit is not borne out by the record, as the 
benefit has been determined from the income tax returns and tax computations of the sampled 
producers/exporters, which show the taxable income and the tax paid thereon. 


96. As regards injury and causal link, the Authority has not relied upon the information in 
the application alone. The determination is based on the transaction-wise import data of DG 
Systems and the verified information of the domestic industry, as examined in the relevant 
sections above, wherein the increase in the market share of the subject imports, the price 
undercutting and price suppression, and the effect of the contraction in demand have been dealt 
with. The landed value has been determined as the CIF value of the imports with the applicable 
basic customs duty, if any, in accordance with the consistent practice of the Authority. Anti- 
dumping duty is not added to the landed value for the purpose of determining price undercutting 
or the injury margin. The non-injurious price is based on the confidential cost information of the 
domestic industry, and the methodology adopted for its determination has been stated in the 
relevant section above. Dumping and subsidisation of the same imports are not mutually 
exclusive, and the finding of injury in the mid-term review for the same period does not preclude 
a finding that the subsidised imports have caused injury to the domestic industry. The law 
addresses the concurrent application of the two duties at the stage of levy, and the Authority has,

as recorded in the relevant section above and in the recommendation, provided that the export 
subsidy component of the countervailing duty be collected only to the extent that it exceeds the 
anti-dumping duty leviable. The confidentiality claims of the domestic industry have been 
examined in the relevant section above. As regards Cheviot Company Ltd., the applicant 
producers have not imported the subject goods from the subject countries during the period of 
investigation and that they are not related to any exporter or importer of the subject goods, and 
no evidence to the contrary has been placed on record; the standing of the applicants has been 
examined in the relevant section above. The request for termination of the investigation in terms 
of Article .9 of the ASCM is accordingly not acceded to. 


L. CONCLUSIONS 


97. Having regard to the contentions raised, information provided and submissions made by 
the interested parties and the facts available before the Authority, as recorded in these final 
findings, and on the basis of the above analysis of the state of subsidisation, injury and causal 
link, the Authority concludes that: 


i. The product under consideration is "Jute Products" comprising jute yarn/twine (single, 
multiple folded or cabled), jute sacking bags and cloth, and jute hessian bags and fabrics, 
including the subject goods when imported as jute products containing mineral oil or 
vegetable oil and as diversified jute products, as defined in the initiation notification, and 
the product produced by the domestic industry is like article to the product under 
consideration. 


il. The applicant producers constitute the domestic industry within the meaning of Rule 2(b) of 
the Rules and the application satisfies the requirement of standing under Rule 6(3) of the 
Rules. 


ii. The Government of Bangladesh filed a response to the government questionnaire, which has 
been taken on record and examined. The programmes of the Government of Bangladesh 
have been examined on the basis of the said response, the information furnished by the 
responding producers/exporters and the facts available on record. The response of the 
Government of Nepal has been taken on record and examined. 


iv. The producers/exporters of the subject goods in Bangladesh have received countervailable 
subsidies under Programme 8 (cash incentive on export of jute goods), which is a prohibited 
export subsidy, and under Programme 40 (preferential income tax treatment of the jute 
industry). No benefit has been established under Programmes | to 7, 9, ll and 2 for the 
sampled producers/exporters. 


v. The producers/exporters of the subject goods in Nepal have received countervailable 
subsidies under Programme | (cash grants on export of jute products), which is a prohibited 
export subsidy, and under Programme 2 (tax subsidies for jute industries). 


vi. The subsidy margins determined for the sampled producers/exporters, the non-sampled 
cooperating producers/exporters and all other producers/exporters from each of the subject 
countries are above the de minimis level. 


vii. The domestic industry has suffered material injury. The subject imports have increased in 
absolute terms and in relation to production and consumption in India over the injury 
period, are undercutting the prices of the domestic industry and have suppressed and 
depressed its prices, and the domestic industry has suffered a decline in production, capacity 
utilisation, domestic sales, market share, profits, cash profits and return on capital 
employed. 


92 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART I—SEc. !] 


viii. The material injury to the domestic industry has been caused by the subsidised imports from 
the subject countries, and the other known factors examined have not caused the injury. 


ix. The subject goods are already subject to anti-dumping duty. In order to ensure that the same 
situation of export subsidisation is not compensated twice, the component of the 
countervailing duty attributable to the export contingent programmes is to be collected only 
to the extent that it exceeds the anti-dumping duty leviable on the same consignment, the 
component attributable to the tax concessions being collected in full. 


x. The imposition of countervailing duty is in the public interest, having regard to the interests 
of the domestic producers, the workers and the raw jute farmers dependent on the industry, 
the absence of any participation by importers or users, and the capacity of the Indian 
industry to meet the demand in the country. 


M. RECOMMENDATION 


98. The Authority notes that the investigation was initiated and notified to all interested 
parties and adequate opportunity was given to the domestic industry, the Governments of the 
subject countries, the producers/exporters, importers and other interested parties to provide 
information on the aspects of subsidisation, injury and causal link. Having initiated and 
conducted the investigation into subsidisation, injury and causal link in terms of the provisions 
of the Act and the Rules, and having established that the producers/exporters of the subject 
goods in the subject countries have received countervailable subsidies within the meaning of 
Section 9 of the Act, that the domestic industry has suffered material injury and that the injury 
has been caused by the subsidised imports, the Authority is of the view that imposition of 
definitive countervailing duty is required to offset the subsidisation and injury. 


99. Having regard to the lesser duty rule followed by the Authority, the Authority 
recommends imposition of definitive countervailing duty equal to the lesser of the subsidy 
margin and the injury margin, so as to remove the injury to the domestic industry. The injury 
margins determined for each of the sampled producers/exporters, the non-sampled cooperating 
producers/exporters and all other producers/exporters from each of the subject countries are 
higher than the corresponding subsidy margins. Accordingly, the Authority recommends 
imposition of definitive countervailing duty on imports of the subject goods originating in or 
exported from the subject countries, for a period of five years from the date of notification by 
the Central Government, as a fixed amount in US dollars per metric tonne for each 
producer/exporter for the product under consideration as a whole. The amount is shown in the 
duty table in two components, that attributable to the export contingent programme (Programme 
8 of Bangladesh and Programme | of Nepal) in column (7) and that attributable to the tax 
concession (Programme l0 of Bangladesh and Programme 2 of Nepal) in column (8), the total 
being shown in column (9). 


200. The subject goods being already subject to anti-dumping duty under Notification No. 
33/2022-Customs (ADD) dated 30th December 2022, the Authority further recommends, in 
terms of Section 9B()(a) of the Act, that the countervailing duty payable on any consignment of 
the subject goods be the amount in column (8) of the duty table together with the amount, if any, 
by which the amount in column (7) exceeds the anti-dumping duty leviable on that consignment 
under the anti-dumping duty notification in force at the time of import; and that where the anti- 
dumping duty so leviable equals or exceeds the amount in column (7), the countervailing duty 
payable be the amount in column (8) alone. The anti-dumping duty shall continue to be collected 
in full.
